records.text: Global Equity Strategy15 June 2026 ab 11 How might this end? In our opinion, there are three major potential outcomes: Potential outcome 1: default. In our view, this is very unlikely given that index-linked debt in the US is just 9% of total debt and thus government debt in theory can be inflated away. Potential outcome 2: wait for a possible bond crisis that result in a U-turn by politicians and fiscal policy being tightened sharply. In our view, there is a 60% chance of this. The reason that it is not higher is that politicians in general have tended to move quite slowly in terms of fiscal policy unless there is a severe financial crisis. Moreover, it is obviously unpopular to tighten fiscal policy. This option could imply that governments end up taxing the corporate sector sharply. The problem with this is that some corporates can move locations to low tax regimes (eg, with the US not signed up to Pillar 2) and corporates often lobby politicians on taxes. Potential outcome 3: central banks intervene to print to fund the deficit. We think there is, at least, a 30% chance of this being the eventual outcome. The logic being that as the Fed cuts rates or keeps rates stable, long term bond yields rise and thus at some point the rise in bond yields hits both growth and equities (1% on the 10-year bond yield, ceteris paribus, takes about 1% off US GDP growth as it normally leads to a 20% fall in US housing starts). records.text: xed investment − and notably construction − which has accounted for virtually all of Italy's growth outperformance since 2019. Fiscal policy has played a central role, most notably through the Superbonus − a housing renovation scheme introduced in 2020 that was used for 3-5% of the housing stock and cost 10½% of GDP . The flipside of this positive growth impulse has been higher budget deficits and debt ratios than in prior decades, even though this did not stand out in international comparison amid the widespread fiscal easing during the pandemic. Over the past two years, the Superbonus has been largely phased out and the headline deficit has narrowed. Yet, construction activity has held up. We attribute this resilience primarily to spending of funds obtained from the EU recovery fund's RRF facility, which also funded a small share of the Superbonus. In total, Italy receives €194bn (8.6% of 2025 GDP) over 2021-26, of which 85% has already been paid out, and 68% of the disbursed funds have been spent so far. According to IMF research, the largest RRF disbursement across all countries and sectors has gone into Italian construction. There is one more tranche to be disbursed from the RRF until end-2026, which, together with the unspent previous disbursements, should still support activity next year, in our view. BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Communication toolkit For much of its history, the BoJ communicated policy in a narrower and less systematic way than it does today. Until the early 1990s, releases centered mainly on official discount rate changes; the money-market operations stance was mostly inferred from the BoJ’s market operations rather than stated in formal releases. This began to change in 1995, when the BoJ started publishing statements that explicitly set out the stance of money market operations. The 1997 revision of the BoJ Act then formalized a broader MPM-centered communication framework, including post-meeting policy statements, regular Governor press conferences, MPM minutes, eventual release of full transcripts with a 10-year lag, and the Semiannual Report to the Diet. records.text: specifying the operations for the following month. • Interpreting Rinban results: Results are primarily assessed using (1) the offer-to- cover ratio and (2) the tail, defined as the spread between the pro rata yield spread and the average accepted yield spread. A high offer-to-cover ratio indicates strong selling demand for JGBs, while a low ratio points to weaker selling interest. As for the tail, because bids are accepted starting from higher yields, a wider tail tends to indicate weaker selling demand. Accordingly, a combination of a low offer-to-cover ratio and a wide tail is typically interpreted as reflecting relatively tight supply– demand conditions in the JGB market and is therefore seen as a positive market signal. • Notification times: The BoJ announces purchase offers at 10:10 JST. The bid submission deadline is 11:40, and results are typically announced around 12:00. • Financial institutions eligible for JGB purchase operations: Institutions with current accounts at the BoJ. This effectively precludes overseas investors from participating directly in BoJ operations.

records.text: Today’s meeting raises the risk of interest rate hikes later this year, but our base case is still that the FOMC will leave the policy rate unchanged this year. A majority could support a hike, perhaps for a range of different reasons, if upcoming inflation prints are uncomfortable and job growth remains solid. Some might be more concerned about recent inflation trends, while others might be less convinced that a hike is necessary but see little harm from a starting point where job growth has been running strong. A great deal will depend on upcoming inflation reports, and we do expect that May core PCE inflation will be firm at 31bp, though 12bp of that would come from financial services. But we suspect that a majority of the twelve voters, as opposed to the nineteen participants, still lean toward an unchanged policy rate. We also suspect that participants treated the news about a deal with Iran and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz cautiously for now. If so, today’s projections could prove stale if trade resumes, which should resolve the most serious source of upside risk to inflation fairly quickly. Warsh noted that “my colleagues around the table, when they submitted their dots, understand the world is changing quite quickly” and will not feel bound by their projections. Higher energy and wage costs have put pressure on businesses, particularly those that are energy/ labour intensive. Weak consumer confidence and macro/ political uncertainty also dampen demand. That said, we note areas of strong performance, with financials particularly a winner, reflecting (i) high savings rate, (ii) supportive rate and market conditions, (iii) government initiatives to support retail investments and (iv) increased financial participation. Even in sectors that are more prone to the pressures in the external environment, it is not all doom and gloom, and there are names where we see attractive opportunities. Financials clear winners in the UK, top picks BARC, NWG, AJB, IGG We continue to be positive on financials. Banks should benefit from a higher for longer rate environment and a steeper yield curve – including via the structural hedge. records.text: Canada Viewpoint | 15 June 2026 7 Market pricing: CORRA indicators We review key means by which to evaluate BoC market pricing across CORRA futures, BoC OIS & CORRA OIS. Our preferred means is to use BoC OIS, which we believe is the cleanest read of BoC expectations. CORRA = overnight risk free repo rate The BoC’s policy target rate is not a market rate, like the Fed’s federal funds rate (FF), but rather a rate they want financial institutions to charge one another to borrow on an overnight basis. To hit that target the BoC adjusts the rate settings on deposits, lending and borrowing tools, or grows/drains asset holdings (more detail in BoC balance sheet: basics & reporting). To know if the BoC is achieving its policy target, they use CORRA. Therefore, looking at market pricing from expectations of CORRA gives the best read for market implied pricing of the BoC policy path. BoC meeting date OIS swaps and CORRA futures make up the foundation of the CAD CORRA swaps curve, where CORRA stands for the Canadian overnight repo rate average. Like SOFR in the US, CORRA is a measure of the cost of overnight general collateral repo funding in CAD Government of Canada (GoC) treasury bills and bonds. The Bloomberg ticker for CORRA is CAONREPO Index. The BoC policy rate has ticker CABROVER Index. CORRA has averaged 2.4bp above CABROVER in the last 6 months. Asymmetrical impact: El Niño effects vary significantly by region and by crop (Figure 23). A Nature Communications study published on 15 May 2014 found that El Niño-Southern Oscillation phases can materially affect areas where staples such as maize, rice, wheat and soya beans are harvested. The findings suggest that El Niño can have a significant but asymmetrical impact on crop yields globally, with negative effects seen in up to 22–24% of harvested area and positive effects in 30–36%. South and SEA most exposed: South and South East Asia are likely to be among the most affected regions, in our view, with risks concentrated in rice, sugar, palm oil, maize and coffee. The region accounts for almost 60% of global rice production and over 80% of global rice exports, with India alone producing close to 30% of the world’s rice. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 9 Exhibit 7: Estimates of Japan’s natural rate of interest (R*) BoJ estimates put R* at roughly -0.9% to +0.5% Source: Bank of Japan, BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH The Phillips curve as organizing principle The broader assessment can be organized around the logic of the Phillips curve. Policy changes affect financial conditions, which in turn feed through to real-economy demand and supply conditions. Those conditions, together with inflation expectations, shape price formation. Japan’s Phillips curve has historically been very flat, so improvement in the output gap alone tends to move inflation only weakly. This raises the importance of inflation expectations and makes stabilizing underlying inflation around 2% the central challenge. The framework can be read through three linked questions: (1) is policy transmitting through financial conditions? (2) how much slack remains? and (3) is price pressure materializing and likely to persist? Studies have shown that El Niño’s effects on northern East Asia is usually differs from southern and central East Asia, making the net impact on the region less straightforward and unpredictable. Wetter Europe provides limited relief: Europe sees a different trend than that in Asia, with a positive correlation between the Niño 3.4 Index and monthly rainfall anomaly. We find that the relationship is the strongest with a six-month lag, aligning with ECMWF’s view that the El Niño impact on Europe tends to be stronger in winter. We hence see potential for higher rainfall at the end of the year going into H1 2027 due to the developing phase of El Niño. However, Southern Europe and the Nordics – where 62% of Europe’s hydropower capacity sits – see weaker correlation than NWE (page 9). We hence see limited increase in hydro generation in the region due to El Niño and think the focus remains on gas generation. We estimate that approximately U$$134bn in passive assets under management (AUM) currently tracks various MSCI benchmark indices that incorporate Chinese equities. Within the Hang Seng index suite, the flagship Hang Seng Index (HSI) and the Hang Seng TECH Index (HSTECH) command the largest passive investor bases, with $28 billion and $24 billion in tracking AUM, respectively. Consequently, potential index inclusion serves as a catalyst, driving passive capital inflows that structurally support post-listing stock performance. Inclusion in the Southbound Stock Connect program provides Hong Kong-listed companies with direct access to vast onshore mainland liquidity. Press conference To increase transparency and forward guidance, the Fed began holding press conferences at every other meeting beginning in April 2011. Then Chair Powell increased the cadence of pressers to one-per-meeting, beginning in December 2018. In the press conference, the Chair aims to represent the views of the committee around what was discussed during the meeting. Research suggests that the press conference generates more rates volatility than the press release. So the market sees the conference as having more information content than the press release. FOMC minutes The Fed also releases meeting minutes three weeks after each meeting. The minutes can give additional color to the press release and press conference. But we often find they offer little new information since so many Fed participants speak following a meeting. The minutes are also sometimes stale, because there are important data releases in the three weeks before they are released. We close our M26 1s5s INR NDOIS steepener trade idea, as we think recent announcements from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has changed the near-term outlook for INR rates. We initiated the trade in March, based on the expectation that rising oil prices would put upward pressure on rates, while fiscal subsidies and a mismatch in bond demand and supply would steepen the curve (see EM rates: Take profit on INR 5y payer, enter 1s5s steepener, dated 11 March). Our view was also supported by the view that front-end pricing of rate hikes seemed extreme relative to core inflation, which remained under control in India. Although there was some chatter that the central bank may hike rates to curb FX depreciation, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) voted unanimously to keep policy rates unchanged in June. Instead, it introduced several FX measures—including 100% hedging-cost support for foreign-currency non-resident (FCNR) deposits and subsidized hedging for external commercial borrowings (ECB) and overseas foreign-currency borrowings (OFCB), with tenors ranging from 3-5 years. The Fed’s communication toolkit includes: the official policy statement after each meeting, the press conference conducted by the Fed Chair following meetings, the quarterly Summary of Economic Projections, Congressional testimonies by the Chair, speeches by Governors and regional Presidents, and media appearances. Chair Warsh is likely to reduce the scope of communication. He thinks it makes the Fed less nimble. Frameworks: a range of rule inputs The Fed uses many inputs in assessing the policy stance. These include Taylor Rules, output and unemployment gaps, financial conditions, estimates of r* and forward- looking assessments of the balance of risks to its mandates. In forecasting Fed policy, we track these metrics, follow the data flow and assess risks based on our forecasts. But it’s also worth noting that the Fed exercises substantial discretion in policymaking. records.text: US Viewpoint | 14 June 2026 11 Action calculation: FF futures are more complicated vs FOMC OIS to back out expected Fed action. We generally view FF futures as 1 of 2 types: (1) clean months (2) unclean months. Clean months do not include a FOMC meeting date, unclean months do. Bloomberg WIRP provides a similar calculation to what is reflected below (Exhibit 16). “Clean” example: to back out market expectations for the July FOMC (July 29), market participants can simply use the implied rate from the August FF futures contract. August does not have Fed meeting, so the implied rate gives a clear read on expectations for the July meeting (it is a clean month, assuming no intermeeting action). The average market pricing for the July FOMC is 100 less Aug FF futures (100 – 96.345 = 3.655%). “Unclean” example: both September & October contain FOMC meetings (Sept 16 & Oct 28). Neither month is clean. To back out market pricing, one must then adjust for the # days prior to the meeting using the old rate & # days with a potentially new rate. The specific calculation is: Market rate = implied FF after meeting * a + FF before meeting * b Where: a = % days in month after FOMC, b = % days in month before FOMC The implied FF rate after the meeting can then be stated as: Implied FF after meeting = (current market rate – FF before meeting * b) / a Once the implied FF rate post meeting has been determined, the probability of a rate hike implied can then be calculated. If the bond yield reflects a rise in growth rather default risk, then the rise in growth rate is offset by the rise in the discount rate. Moreover, the discount rate for corporate debt is obviously the corporate bond yield (not the government bond yield - often rising government bond yields are associated with falling credit spreads). The headline business conditions index fell 13.9 points to 5.7 in June, below its 6- month average. Demand and production continued to show strength and resilience. The shipments index decreased 10.3 points to 8.6, remaining firmly positive and extending the strength seen in the prior month. The new orders index fell 19.2 points to 3.5, , remaining modestly positive and consistent with continued demand growth. Both indices were very strong in the prior month, therefore some moderation was to be expected, and we do not view the decline as evidence of softening regional manufacturing activity. Labor demand from manufacturers remained in expansion territory. The index for number of employees edged down to 8.3, but still marked a fifth consecutive month of expansion. The average workweek index fell to 5.1, although it remained at a healthy level. Overall, the latest developments further strengthen our existing view of resilience. Our macroeconomic forecasts (see our Global Outlook) have been conditioned on a smoothed oil price path that saw Brent average USD110/bbl in Q2, declining to USD85/bbl by year-end. Assuming the current spot of about USD78/bbl persists through the rest of June, this would leave the average price around 12% lower than assumed. This is meaningful, but not a game changer. Our previous analysis on the macroeconomic impact of oil price changes suggested that a 10% move in oil prices was worth around 0.1pp on GDP and about 0.4pp on headline inflation. This assumes a permanent shift in the level of oil prices, though. In practice, we are simply arriving at our year-end forecast earlier than anticipated. The mechanical effects on inflation – through lower energy prices over the next 3 –6 months – will likely be more significant than the implications for economic activity. That said, we would caution against assuming the inflationary episode is over. After all, the first-order inflationary impulse is already baked in. ariffs. The EU is lacking a trade defence instrument capable of dealing with systemic overcapacities. Thus, the EU might discuss enhancing its toolkit with a trade defence instrument that could mirror US section 301 tariffs, a new “overcapacity tool”. Any potential new EU trade defence tool would likely allow for "ex officio" investigations into perceived unfair trade practices to be initiated by the EU Commission. A set of criteria would define "systemic overcapacities" and the harm done to EU industries. If such harm were to be found in the EU's investigation, the EU Commission would then be able to levy additional tariffs, impose quotas or market access restrictions on entire sectors instead of only individual products. Consensus likely to be strongest around option two. In terms of political feasibility, progress is likely to be fastest on making greater use of existing EU trade defence tools (anti-dumping and anti-subsidy investigations), also by adding staff to the investigation teams at the EU Commission. With respect to the new “diversification instrument” progress is expected to be slower. Although we expect general political buy-in for a legislative proposal to expand the trade defence toolbox, building any new instrument does not mean that such tools will then also actually be used. records.text: Global Strategy15 June 2026 ab 2 Introduction to the Momentum strategy What is the Momentum strategy? An equity momentum strategy is one of the most widely used investment approaches, built on a simple but powerful principle: stocks that have performed well recently tend to continue outperforming, while those that have lagged tend to keep underperforming. Why does it work? The intuition behind its success is twofold: first, behavioral biases lead investors to underreact to new information; second, the gradual diffusion of information, such as earnings or macro developments, means it takes time to be fully reflected in prices. How has it performed in the past, relative to the index? Since 1927, the momentum strategy has outperformed the S&P , delivering a Sharpe ratio of 0.80 versus 0.63 for the index. Over the same period, the long/short market- neutral implementation achieved a Sharpe ratio of 0.42, offering strong diversification benefits. The recent outperformance has drawn increased investor attention and raised questions about its sustainability. However, it appears to have been primarily earnings- driven, with valuations compressing since Q3 of last year. With central bank buying at best an indeterminate influence during this time, the fundamental new news was arguably net negative for gold. records.text: Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market has experienced a powerful resurgence, with more than 60 new listings making their debut ytd. Newly listed companies have delivered strong post-IPO performance, +45%/49%/67% on average in the first trading day/first month/three months post-listing, although with significant performance dispersion. We highlight 3 strategies to trade for alpha in this market. Factors driving post-IPO returns: Standalone, large-cap listings consistently 1. outperform small-caps and dual-listed peers. High retail oversubscription serves as a primary catalyst for short-term price appreciation, while moderate cornerstone ownership of 30% to 50% signals high-quality listings positioned for sustainable outperformance. Over extended horizons exceeding 3 months, structural outperformance is concentrated in high-growth New Economy sectors. Lock-Up Expiration Risks: The HK market may see US$274bn of potential new 2. supply from shares due to post-IPO lock-up expiration. Historical precedents indicate a moderate price decline of 4% to 7% within three to six months post-release accompanied by high return dispersion. Near-term post-expiration performance is primarily determined by the volume of released lock-up shares relative to outstanding shares. Conversely, medium-term returns are structurally driven by the post-release free float ratio and the stock’s pre-expiration performance. records.text: US Viewpoint | 14 June 2026 7 measures the Fed looks at to try and gauge whether its policy setting is appropriate. These include the following: 1. Policy rules: Monetary policy rules like the original Taylor Rule can provide snapshot assessments of where policy rates should be set based on current economic conditions. The Fed tends to treat these “rules” more like guidelines, typically exercising substantial discretion in policy setting. Additionally, a certain rule may map the Fed policy setting framework well during certain periods, but poorly at other times. 2. Financial conditions: Fed policy is transmitted to the economy through financial conditions. Raising short-term borrowing rates should push all interest rates higher, which should slow investment and consumption, all else equal. That should also put downward pressure on equities. Therefore, financial conditions measures can provide evidence of whether the Fed is in restrictive territory or not. These measures are imperfect, however, since other factors affect interest rates across the curve and equity market performance can be driven by idiosyncratic factors such as the positive outlook for AI. 3. Output and employment gaps: When the output (GDP vs. potential) or unemployment gap (the natural unemployment rate vs. actual) is positive, the Fed should set policy in a restrictive setting to cool the economy and prevent inflation. If either of these gaps continues to widen, it can signal that the Fed should raise rates

records.text: UK Economics and Rates 15 June 2026 Citi Research 2 The Bank of England’s MPC is once again facing headwinds from both directions. On the one hand, underlying real variables are weakening. Unemployment is rising; real wage growth is slowing down; and productivity and output are barely growing. On the other hand, the Committee wants to avoid a repeat of the previous inflationary episode from a couple of years ago, when the cost-push shock led to strong second-round effects, de-anchored inflation expectations, and a wage- price spiral ensued. We discuss four things. First, we’ll give a strategic read for why we think the Committee will be holding rates for the June policy decision, and indeed for the remainder of this calendar year and early next. Second, we’ll turn to key components in the data we think members on the MPC will point to in justifying this hold. Third, we’ll discuss upside risks to our assessment and the conditions which would lead the MPC to hike rates. Finally, we’ll examine how fiscal policy can impact monetary policy outcomes. Maintaining the ‘Active’ Hold Our base case is that the MPC holds Bank Rate at 3.75% for the remainder of 2026, and the hawkish bark dominating their communications is bigger than the bite. We expect Megan Greene to join Huw Pill as a second dissenter voting for a 25bps hike in the upcoming June meeting. We assume each 10% increase in the oil price takes c0.1% off GDP . 3) The rise in fertiliser prices. We are past peak planting season, thus food prices look set to rise c8-10%, which we believe could add 50bps to inflation. 4) ECB raising one one more occasion. UBS sees the ECB raising on one more occasion (taking rates up by 50bps, in aggregate), and we assume each 50bps increase in rates takes, with a lag, 0.5% off GDP growth. Last week, the ECB meeting raised core inflation forecasts for 2026 and 2027 to 2.5%, and for 2028 to 2.2%; and recent comments implied that the rate hike was not pre-emptive. The offsets for weaker growth would be higher wage growth, a fall in the saving ratio and some fiscal easing. These offsets look limited: the ECB wage trackers show very little rise in wage growth, and fiscal easing so far has been just 0.1% of GDP , but we expect it to rise to 0.5% of GDP (cf. to 3% of GDP over Ukraine). Hence, we can see GDP in Europe has been revised down more than any region since the conflict started. records.text: Global Strategy15 June 2026 ab 10 'Supportive': Momentum strategies offer meaningful tail-hedging benefits, a feature that is consistently valued within a portfolio Periods of elevated market uncertainty have often favoured momentum rather than undermined it. In nine episodes since 1920 when the S&P fell more than 20%, momentum ranked among the top five performers in six cases, including the Great Depression and the Global Financial Crisis (Figure 11). This reflects its long-winner/short- loser structure, allowing it to benefit from strong dispersion during prolonged bear markets. The greater risk to momentum arises during recoveries, not drawdowns. Many of its largest losses occur near market bottoms, when previously underperforming stocks rebound sharply as risk appetite returns, such as in 1932 and 2009 (Figure 18M o m e n t u m h a s t y p i c a l l y s t r u g g l e d w h e n m a r k e t s r e b o u n d r a t h e r t h a n d u r i n g t h e d o w n t u r n , see also Daniel and Moskowitz 2016). records.text: ain given the weakness of the real economy. The data justifying the hold Two aspects of the data point to why the MPC will vote to hold rates in June. (1) Nominal prices are more subdued and (2) the real economy is weaker. Prices and their expectations are more subdued – Unlike the false dawn of the past two years, a clear signal in the recent UK data has emerged, and this one appears to have substance beneath it. Core CPI fell to its lowest level in nearly 5 years; headline CPI in April undershot expectations slowing down to 2.8% in April, from 3.3% in March. Crucially, services inflation – the domestically generated, wage-sensitive measure the Bank treats as the truest read of underlying pressure – also fell. (Admittedly, there were large base effects in April so some of this weakness is attributable to that.) In as much as there was inflationary pressure, this was concentrated in liquid fuels. Whilst it is now the steepest rise mid-2022, the fact it is yet to seep into other components of inflation is good news for the Bank of England. This conflict-driven effect, pulling headline the other way, is really the primary reason the Bank of England still expects headline to grind back to 3.3% in 2026Q3.1 Figure 1. records.text: swaps market that spans the period between BoJ meetings (meeting-date OIS). Implied policy expectations are derived from the fixed rate consistent with compounded TONA over the period from the business day following the previous meeting to the final day of the subsequent meeting. For example, for the June 15–16 meeting, the relevant swap rate reflects the expected compounded TONA from the business day following the April 27–28 meeting through June 16, and therefore serves as a proxy for the degree of market-implied policy rate changes priced into that meeting. In practice, however, the calculation is typically simplified by using the current level of TONA rather than fully compounding daily fixings. More concretely, the implied probability of a rate hike can be approximated by taking the spread between the fixed rate and TONA and dividing it by the BoJ’s standard policy increment of 25bp. For example: • Fixed rate: 0.959% • TONA: 0.727% Rate hike pricing ≒ (Implied rate − TONA) / 0.25 = (0.959 − 0.727) / 0.25 ≒ 92.8%. Such market-implied policy probabilities can be tracked via Bloomberg’s World Interest Rate Probability (WIRP) function (WIRP JP). This was not a single numerical target, but an aggregation of Policy Board members’ views on the CPI inflation rate consistent with price stability: roughly a 0–2% range, with most members’ central values around 1%, reviewed annually. In February 2012, under Governor Shirakawa, the Bank replaced the “Understanding” with a “Price Stability Goal in the Medium to Long Term” (中長期的な物価安定の目途), defined as 2% or lower in positive territory, with 1% set as the goal “for the time being.” In January 2013, amid strong external pressure including from the government, the Bank adopted a single 2% “Price Stability Target” (物価安定の目標). records.text: ab 15 June 2026 Global Research Global Equity Strategy Bonds: What if? What is the risk of further rises in bond yields and what should we do if the risk unfolds? Bonds - what if and what to do UBS forecasts the US 10-year bond yield to fall to 4.25% by year-end. We struggle to see the current sell-off in bonds continuing with: i) the 1-year rate implied in 10 years' time at 5.2% (higher than the neutral rate); ii) there is normally a very tight fit between changes in the 2-year note yield and changes in the 10-year TIPS yield and UBS expects no rate hike this year (versus the market pricing in a rate hike by year-end) - there are good reasons for this, as we highlight here; iii) no further fiscal easing in the US; and iv) a potential near-term resolution in the Middle East. What’s the long-term risk for bonds? The risk in our view is that: i) governments are facing, on some measures, a record rise in populism and hence now appear prone to spend - our concern is that this continues until bond yields rise to levels that risk an economic crisis (in the late 80's, we recall that the most important monthly print was the US Treasury monthly statement) - this year Japan and EZ are easing fiscal policy to combat higher energy prices, while the US has the OBBB; ii) the fiscal position is already problematic for the UK, US and France. For the KRW and JPY, we think efforts to strengthen the currency may prove short- lived if fundamentals don’t align (in the JPY’s case), or foreign investor outflows don’t abate (in the KRW’s case). For the TWD, the central bank aims to keep the currency from breaking meaningfully to either side of its range. Meanwhile, we see the widening of the South Korea and Taiwan current accounts as more sustainable than that of Japan’s, which has been largely driven by interest and dividend income. KEY MESSAGES We believe flow dynamics help explain why the JPY, KRW and TWD remain relatively weak despite improvements in their currency account balances and gains in local equities. Foreign investor flows skew most bearish for the KRW, while domestic institutional and retail flows skew more bearish for the JPY and TWD. While smoothing action from authorities may create two-way risks, we expect the flow dynamics will continue to underpin these currencies’ use as funders even if a durable peace is achieved in the Middle East. The JPY remains our preferred funder in North Asia, with fundamentals and flows weighing on the currency. The trend towards globalisation, supported by both political and technological developments, allowed a significant outsourcing of lower-skilled manufacturing jobs from Western economies. Between 1990 and 2009, the share of labour compensation in national income fell in 26 out of 30 advanced countries, with the median labour share of national income falling from 66.1% to 61.7%, according to the OECD. Rapid migration also contributed to this effect. In the UK, for example, the relative price of labour fell by around 20% between 2009 and 2015 as the labour supply increased by almost 4 million or 12.5%, according to the ONS. Meanwhile, there was also a meaningful decline in energy costs. Significant investment in the 1990s and 2000s meant that there was excess capacity in commodity exploration in the post financial crisis era. Third, in the post pandemic era of higher inflation alongside higher nominal GDP , we began to see a structural improvement in revenue growth in many industries which have long been overlooked by investors and where there had been a lack of investment over a long period of time. After the financial crisis, when growth was scarce, areas that could grow with a high degree of certainty were highly prized, particularly given historically low discount rates. By contrast, the so-called old economy companies were widely overlooked. They suffered from overcapacity in many cases, and, because of the financial crisis, declining returns. There has been a notable shift in the valuation of physical assets, as the fortunes of the virtual and physical worlds have become intertwined for the first time since the rollout and commercialisation of the Internet (Exhibit 28). The growth opportunities for many technology companies are no longer a function of finding solutions to problems in the virtual world through apps and software. Instead, future growth has become increasingly dependent on the physical infrastructure around them. Data centres and energy suppliers have become crucial to their growth plans, leading to a cascading effect where capex spending by the tech giants has spilled into improved growth opportunities across many traditional, value-oriented, old economy industries that had long been overlooked. records.text: 2 Canada Viewpoint | 15 June 2026 Bank of Canada overview The Bank of Canada’s mandate The Bank of Canada is Canada’s (BoC) central bank. Its mandate, as set out in the Bank of Canada Act, is “to promote the economic and financial welfare of Canada.” The BoC fulfills this mandate through four core functions. In monetary policy, it seeks to maintain low, stable, and predictable inflation. In terms of the financial system, it works to support safe, sound, and efficient financial systems both within Canada and globally. Its currency function involves designing, issuing, and distributing Canada’s bank notes. In funds management, the Bank serves as the fiscal agent for the Government of Canada, overseeing public debt programs and managing foreign exchange reserves. The Bank of Canada’s mandate in practice The BoC has followed an explicit inflation-targeting regime since 1991, one of the first central banks to do it, with a flexible exchange rate. Canada’s monetary policy framework is based on two main elements: an inflation-control target and a flexible exchange rate. The inflation control framework centers on a 2% inflation target and is both symmetric— treating deviations above and below the target equally—and flexible, as decisions are guided by expected inflation over a six - to eight- quarter horizon relative to the 2% target and within a 1%–3% range. records.text: s. To understand why, note that negative supply shocks raise both unemployment and inflation, while positive supply shocks do the opposite. Therefore, in responding to supply shocks, the Fed must decide which of its mandates it is more concerned about and accept the risk that in addressing this concern it might be exacerbating the shock to the other mandate. The 2% target was officially adopted in 2012 In January 2012, under Chair Bernanke, the Fed officially adopted a 2% PCE inflation target for its price stability mandate. While the Fed didn’t have an explicit target until 2012, it implicitly targeted 2% inflation beginning in 1996. Members of the Fed suggest there were two reasons the Fed didn’t adopt the 2% target sooner: 1) Chair Greenspan thought a target might limit the Fed’s discretion on policy, and 2) the Fed worried a target would force it to be more hawkish in periods of slightly elevated inflation. The official adoption of the 2% target led Fed forecasts of inflation in the final year of its projections to be much more tightly clustered around 2% (Exhibit 2). Why 2%? He made the point that since the zero-lower-bound is a constraint for nominal rates, the 2% target gave the Fed more room to cut and support the economy, pushing real rates into negative territory if needed. records.text: The rapid innovation in large language models and advances in agentic AI have raised concerns about disruption to technology business models (Exhibit 24). Investors are keen to avoid the AI era’s version of Kodak, IBM, Nokia, Blackberry and a host of other companies that saw their business models challenged by new waves of innovation (Exhibit 25 and Exhibit 26). In just a couple of months, the value of the software sector fell by around 5 PE points globally, as investors raised the risk premium associated with future projected cash flows and implicitly reduced the terminal value assumptions. The software and IT sector traded at a roughly 100% premium relative to the global market excluding tech less than 5 years ago, whereas the hardware and IT equipment sector enjoyed a premium of less than 20%. Now, they have converged. For the first time in a generation, investors started to question the value of long duration growth companies’ terminal values which had been previously boosted by solid confidence in their ability to sustain premium growth alongside historically low discount rates (Exhibit 27). records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 15 Exhibit 13 illustrates the balance sheet effects for the FEFSA, the BoJ, and financial institutions in the case of a US$-selling/yen-buying intervention. As a first step, dollar funds held in the FEFSA are paid to financial institutions in exchange for yen, leading to a decline in financial institutions’ current account balances at the BoJ. From the BoJ’s perspective, this decline is offset by a corresponding increase in government deposits. As a second step, the FEFSA uses the yen proceeds from the dollar sale to redeem a corresponding amount of FBs.1 This reduces financial institutions’ holdings of FBs while increasing their current account balances at the BoJ. On the BoJ’s balance sheet, this appears as a decline in government deposits and an increase in financial institutions’ current account balances. In net terms, the impact of FX intervention on BoJ current account balances offsets, leaving no change in the monetary base. As a result, FX interventions are effectively sterilized by construction under the current institutional arrangement. We wrote on this issue at length last week and will try to avoid repeating ourselves too much now. But the essence of our argument was that we feel it’s unlikely that new Fed Chair Warsh will adopt a more aggressive approach. UBS economists expect 6 or more of the 19 FOMC members to signal in their 2026 “dots” that at least one rate hike is appropriate this year. With the market priced for 21bp of hikes by end-2026, this would not be controversial in itself. While Warsh could potentially join a smaller group seeing rate cuts as appropriate, doing so by using any press conference to promote a more dovish perspective risks losing capital with the hawkish group at a time when data provide a logic for being open minded about rate hikes. And while the fall in oil prices since the MoU deal is welcome, it seems too soon for policymakers to conclude forcefully that this factor will persist in a helpful direction. After all, as the relatively modest decline in US 10 year yields from last week’s highs shows, there are other factors such as the AI investment boom and record highs in equity markets that also argue in favour of monetary tightening, not least given recent strong US jobs data. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 13 Against this backdrop, the BoJ’s balance sheet—after expanding significantly under former Governor Kuroda—has entered a contraction phase. Reflecting reduced purchases and ongoing redemptions, the Bank’s JGB holdings have been declining gradually. In June 2025, the BoJ formally decided to scale back JGB purchases, and an interim assessment of this process was conducted at the June 2026 MPM. Under the current plan, purchase reductions will continue through January-March 2027, after which further JGB purchase reductions are expected to be paused. However, as JGB redemptions are projected to exceed purchase amounts thereafter, the balance sheet is likely to continue shrinking. In line with these developments, the BoJ’s operational toolkit has also been streamlined. At present, regular JGB purchase operations (Rinban operations) and the Securities Lending Facility (SLF) constitute the main balance sheet-related instruments. These measures help mitigate the side effects associated with the large-scale asset purchases implemented under former Governor Kuroda. Rinban operations The BoJ’s JGB purchase operations involve supplying funds to the market through outright JGB purchases, with no condition that the bonds will be resold after a set period. Purchases were previously conducted via either competitive auctions or fixed- rate purchases. Furthermore, media readings on Warsh are generally hawkish relative to Powell, pushing back on the view that the Chair will be automatically dovish because of political bias. Overall, this suggests policy will be kept balanced at the 17 June meeting, with no change to rates or balance sheet policy. BoJ’s hawkish hike The BoJ raised rates to a 31 -year high and pledged to maintain steady government bond purchases. Its forward guidance suggested that further hikes remain possible, depending on the outlook; hawkish, but still conditional. Our central bank tone measure through this week shows the BoJ remains relatively dovish versus the FOMC. After the meeting, investors did not appear convinced that another hike was likely in the coming months. As a result, USDJPY may continue to struggle to move lower in the near term, barring government intervention. RBA: Possibly too restrictive The RBA unanimously voted to keep rates unchanged at its 16 June meeting. Governor Michele Bullock noted that inflation risks remain two-sided and that activity is still broadly tracking the Bank’s forecasts. records.text: Buy KDP €4.728s of 2035 and KDP €4.224s of 2032 either outright or by swapping out of JDEPNA As we recently discussed in (HG Consumer Products, Food & Beverage: Actions to Support IG ratings, M&A Updates and Pockets of Value), we view the KDP Maple € bonds as offering the most value on the KDP/JDEPNA curve. We recommend buying the KDP €4.728s of 2035 either outright or by swapping out of the JDEPNA €2034s, and we recommend buying the KDP €4.224s of 2032 either outright or by swapping out of the JDEPNA €2033s. In the first trade, we see room to pick up close to 30bp, and in the second, a little over 20bp. As of May 21, the company had completed all actions to ensure that all of its debt, including the new KDP Maple bonds and the bonds issued by JDEP , was structurally pari passu through the addition of KDP Maple, KDP parent, and KDP subsidiary guarantees - with the KDP parent and subsidiary guarantees expected to fall away following the separation, leaving the KDP Maple and JDEP debt pari with one another as part of the coffee company structure, and expected to remain as such (comprising the KDP Maple/coffeeco debt stack) post the separation. The split of the coffee business remains on track for early 2027 and we estimate that at YE26, net leverage should stand around 4.9x giving partial equity credit for private credit investments and 4.5x on a company basis. We find little predictive power from low volatility to future returns, but persistently lower volatility does improve AUD’s carry-to-volatility metrics, which historically have been associated with a stronger AUDUSD path. Similarly, AUD risk reversals have stabilised around their historical average after reaching elevated levels in Q1 during the global reflation trade, and depressed levels in the early phase of the Iran-US conflict. So, the technical excesses that characterised the AUD rally earlier in the year have been washed out, with positioning, carry metrics, and risk reversals all pointing to a more balanced technical backdrop for the AUD. records.text: Metals & Mining Equity View: Stay selective in miners: For mining equities, we stay selective, focusing on stock-specific leverage rather than a top-down call on the space. Our covered names still offer meaningful exposure to moves in gold, but valuation matters: we continue to prefer Endeavour and Hochschild on cheaper multiples and lower implied gold prices, see Boliden as the most levered base-metals exposure to gold, and think Fresnillo looks most vulnerable given its fuller valuation starting point. Within our global coverage, Newmont Mining and Agnico Eagle Mines, both rated OW, are our preferred names to gain exposure. Equity Derivatives view: Gold down from ‘h(e)aven’; reset reveals skew dislocations: Gold’s pullback reflects a technical reset following an overstretched, bubble-like rally. Positioning and option metrics have normalised from extremes, most notably skew, with calls now screening unusually cheap vs. ATM in a full reversal from earlier in the year, while put skew has richened on renewed hedging demand. Higher real yields and persistent inflation continueto present near-term headwinds, even as structural support remains intact. The cleaner technical backdrop and pronounced skew dislocations therefore make options a more efficient way to express both downside risks and asymmetric upside re-engagement, should geopolitical risks subside. 15 June 2026 2 Barclays | Cross-Asset Research

Further, weather agencies have forecast Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomalies to be much higher than previous El Niño events. Indeed, the latest weekly Niño 3.4 index reading was already at 0.7°C, while during the 2023–24 El Niño event, the index had peaked at 2.1°C in late November. According to the US Climate Prediction Center, there is a 63% chance of a very strong El Niño during November–January. El Niño events typically start to develop in May and peak in November/December before tapering off into next April/May. El Niño, especially a strong one, could see higher temperatures this year across the world, as well as a milder winter, with precipitation levels also likely to be affected. Effects could vary across different regions and materialise at different times due to a multitude of factors, including geographical location relative to the Pacific Ocean. The Governor gives multiple formal speeches each year, anchored around a regular domestic circuit of business leader meetings, with additional appearances at policy conferences and international events. The Deputy Governors and other Policy Board members typically give two to four speeches a year each, often at regional events with local business leaders. Speeches are often followed by a press conference or Q&A. Signal weight varies by speaker, as discussed in the Board Composition section. The Governor’s speeches carry the most weight as the leadership view, while Uchida’s are high signal by virtue of their rarity. Speeches by other Policy Board members are primarily read for individual policy leanings. In practice, speeches are where most pre‑signaling of policy moves has occurred. Interviews Less frequent than speeches but often higher impact when they happen. The Governor and Deputies give occasional interviews to Nikkei, Reuters, Bloomberg, and major foreign outlets, typically around inflection points in the policy cycle. The interview format is less constrained than a speech and tends to produce more directional language, which makes interviews a meaningful channel for advance signaling. Moreover, food retail specialists suggest at least a 9 month lag between wholesale and retail prices. The aforementioned input costs index was printing around 0%Y this time last year, before entering a double digit deflation in 2H25. Given just how punitive base effects from this time last year are - as food prices in the spring and summer rose sharply on the back of beef and dairy products - and considering soft (spot and lagged) wholesale pressures, it is fair to say that it would have been more puzzling if food prices had evolved in line with the BoE's forecasts from April vs. their realised trajectory between March and May. Note, food inflation is currently 130bp below the BoE's April forecast. Having said all of this, our second point pertains not to the miss vs. the BoE's forecasts, but rather vs. our projections. We had modelled a 0.3%M pick-up in food prices in May, where we got a 0.1%M contraction instead. records.text: Canada Viewpoint | 15 June 2026 13 Overnight standing repo facility: funding backstops The BoC operates an overnight standing repo facility (OSRF), distinct from its standard overnight repo operations. The rate for this facility is set at the top of the target range, known as the Bank Rate, and serves as a backstop for funding pressure. The primary purpose of the overnight standing repo facility is to reinforce the upper limit of funding rates, acting as a ceiling in case of significant funding market volatility. In contrast, overnight and term repo operations are used primarily for fine-tuning CORRA, helping it stay close to the target rate. The OSRF is always available as a backstop and does not operate within a specific auction window. There has been no usage of the facility given the elevated rate. Conversely, overnight repo (OR) operations are conducted at designated morning auction times, around market rates, providing targeted liquidity adjustments. Standing liquidity facility and standing term liquidity facility: liquidity backstop The BoC’s Standing liquidity facility (SLF) and standing term liquidity facility (STLF) are distinct parts of the BoC’s toolkit, not intended to backstop repo, but instead to ensure smooth system functioning and provide liquidity during periods of stress. By contrast, the forward-looking rules, which typically look through short-term movements and target inflation future inflation, are dovish. As such, the case to hike has less to do with spot data per se and more the theoretical framework which individual members wish to apply to their judgements. The difference here is meaningful. By taking the contemporaneous rule (which in simple terms is about inflation persistence and emphasising the inflation path in the immediate future) would require hikes in the near-term. On the other side of this, the forward-looking rules (which are about placing more emphasis on inflation further into the future and therefore ‘looking through’ short- term turbulence) easily accommodates an argument for a hold. As such, even if it turns out that we are in the benign scenario A, the contemporaneous Taylor rules suggest Bank Rate should be ~25bps tighter in 2026Q3. Moreover, if members believe the economic conditions are closer to scenario B or C, then they are also readying for further hikes to quickly bring inflation back to target. records.text: Two More Cuts, but Not for a While Until the war ends and FOMC participants feel confident that the upside risk to inflation it presents is behind us, the Fed’s debate is likely to focus on potential rate hikes. Even then, in light of the large group on the FOMC that has expressed concern about many years of high inflation, we would not expect the FOMC to lower the funds rate until year-over-year core PCE inflation approaches 2%. This is likely to take quite a while, and we have therefore penciled in the final two cuts in June and December 2027. As we noted last week, a long pause would increase the probability that the FOMC could eventually instead conclude that the funds rate is already in an appropriate place if the economy continues to perform well, a conclusion that we would find reasonable but that most FOMC participants have not yet drawn. As a result, we see a flat path as a plausible alternative to our baseline and give it nearly as high a probability in our fed funds scenario analysis. Even so, our probability-weighted Fed forecast is meaningfully more dovish than market pricing, largely reflecting our skepticism of rate hikes (Exhibit 8). However, we believe that markets have already adjusted to price this in, with long MYR positioning having squeezed to neutral levels (according to BNP Paribas Global FX Positioning Tracker), and BNP Paribas BEER+ model suggesting USDMYR fair value closer to 3.95. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: Malaysia’s economy remains resilient as a net energy exporter, though fiscal and political concerns persist. April’s trade surplus came in stronger than expected at MYR28.75bn, versus MYR16.60bn consensus, driven by 36.9% increase in exports (reflecting a surge in electrical and petrochemical exports). While domestic fuel price caps helped suppress headline inflation to 1.9% y/y in April, high subsidies caused the fiscal deficit to widen by 37% y/y. Overall, we see little incentive for Bank Negara Malaysia to change its policy rate. records.text: BofA Global Research estimates BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Careful management of balance sheet and project risk Morgan Sindall has enjoyed a net cash position in the past 10 years, and we expect this to continue, giving it the flexibility to be selective with its pipeline. In its construction services segment, the company usually focuses on small projects with a shorter completion time, and often in public/regulated sectors. These clients typically have a healthier risk profile and the projects are secured with limited competition. Huge mid-term potential to unlock mixed-use profit We see a strong earnings pipeline ahead, especially in its mixed-use business (MUSE). The company has an impressive c.£12bn total secured order book against £5bn revenue expected in 2025. Its order book value for MUSE stood at £4.6bn in 2025, or c.40% of the total order book, while revenue is only at 1%. Revenue growth in MUSE should pick up from 9% in 2026E to 20% in 2028E. Morgan Sindall is one of just a few national players that have the experience and balance sheet to carry out such long-term and complex projects, in our view. The stock now trades in-line with 10Y average at P/E and EV/EBIT of 12x/8x. This we think is very important and informative in the context of last year's vote dissents by Chief Economist Pill, Deputy Governor Lombardelli and external member Greene. Their thesis, as we understood it this time last year, was that the upswing in headline inflation due to food prices in 2H25 might lead to a prolonged inflation overshoot. We had instead thought that an economy with as much spare capacity as the UK will probably not be able to sustain an overshoot, absent inflationary regulatory decisions. That last year's food price shock was digested this smoothly, and that the current energy shock is not immediately spreading beyond fuel prices is encouraging and dovish. We don't, however, expect much of a victory lap from the doves on the MPC, nor a change in view from the hawks. Headline inflation is yet to peak - given the delayed nature of the regulated utility bills increase. Faced with inflation above target, and an upswing in headline inflation - as was the case, for example, in August last year - the BoE tends to down-weight economic and labour market weakness. The focus will remain firmly, we think, on spot inflation, and not what the inflationary process suggests for headline inflation in a years' time. Don’t fade the rebound yet: In the past two years, since the end of the COVID-inflation wave, global credit markets have experienced two major sell-offs: the summer of 2024 (French politics and a VIXplotion) and March 2025 (Liberation Day). After each shock spreads have normalised, but it’s taken at least six months until the next shock. That’s normal behaviour when credit is mid-cycle – credit conditions, fundamental trends, investor behaviour all lacking extremes and being mid-range, creating significant shock absorbers for the market. If the post-Middle East war cycle follows the same pattern – and we think it should – then vulnerability needs complacency, and complacency is when market positioning is firmly long again, and when consensus revises macro expectations positively again. Both trends are underway, but neither is flashing red, or even amber yet (Figure 1). Beyond the war – A hotter cycle is emerging: The war has demonstrated that also the US economy has shock absorbers. records.text: Despite substantial capital demands arising from new listings, post-IPO secondary financing, and lock-up expiration, we anticipate that robust equity demand could be able to absorb this incoming supply. We estimate that total demand for Hong Kong-listed equities could exceed US$400bn. This demand is supported by US$180bn in corporate distributions (comprising dividends and share buybacks), US$$20–30bn in capital reallocation from global long-term institutional investors, US$200bn potential Southbound capital inflows, and additional buying interest from retail investors. Historical precedents suggest that equities typically experience moderate downward price pressure following lock-up expiration, with a median share price decline of 4% in three months and 7% in six months post-release; however, performance exhibits significant divergence across individual issuers. We examined factors that may influence stock performance after lock-up share release. In the near term, the volume of lock-up shares released as a percentage of total outstanding shares serves as the primary determinant of performance (specifically within the first week post-expiration). Conversely, the post-release free float ratio and the stock’s pre-expiration post-IPO performance are the key structural drivers of medium-term returns to the following three- and six-month returns. Companies with high cornerstone ownership, especially domestic ones, tend to observe higher selling pressure after lock-up share release

Our initial take on the print is here. Given the scale of the downside surprise in goods and food prices, most of our conversations with investors today revolved around how sustainable this weakness might be. Our take on this is nuanced. We expect both core goods and food inflation to (gradually) accelerate into year-end, but we don't necessarily read today's data as an oddity or entirely a result of ONS idiosyncracies. Going into this year's energy shock, price pressures in the retail and food retail sectors were contained, and a swift acceleration in core goods and food inflation - as modelled, in the case of food prices, by the BoE - did seem implausible to us. We see downside risks to our very near-term food and core goods forecasts, as informed by today's readings. But we expect both of these categories to tick up into year-end and over 1H27. We take down our modelled peak in food inflation from just under 6%Y, to just below 5%Y, to be attained by mid-2027. The BoE looks likely to have to shave ~2pp off their food inflation forecasts come the July forecast round. What next? For the ECB, recent developments likely take a July hike off the table, but we think a September hike is still more likely than not. This is predicated on the assumption that the conflict in the Middle East is still ongoing by the time of the June vote. The Committee faces a classic stagflationary dilemma: the real economy is showing signs of a cyclical downturn as input costs are also simultaneously accelerating from an exogenous shock. The effect is a bifurcated reality which allows credible hawkish and dovish arguments. Prior to late February 2026, CPI was on a downward trajectory and there was emerging slack in the economy. All else being equal, this narrative still holds. However, as is frequently noted, ceteris is rarely paribus. Since February, the UK has been managing yet another supply-side shock, triggered by the Iran conflict. The ‘textbook economics’ response is to look through this shock, especially if it’s external and transitory. However, the MPC must remain conscious of the past, and the risk of another wage-price spiral and other second-round effects. (This is why they went to incredible lengths in the April MPR to outline the different Taylor rule paths in Annex 1 of the report – more on this below.) records.text: European Economic Perspectives15 June 2026 ab 2 This might be peak Italy, but too early to worry As we approach the end of the NGEU's RRF, where to from here? Overall, we think current Italian economic performance might be "as good as it gets" in the sense that we do not see additional growth drivers kicking in. However, this does not mean that we think growth will falter in the near term. First, while RRF disbursement may end in 2026, we believe there is enough backlog in spending the funds to support growth through 2027, with 2028 being the year where a "fiscal cliff" may loom. Second, 2027 is an election year, risking some volatility and potentially looser fiscal stance, but opinion polls remain relatively stable for now. Third, in the long term, the key question is whether Italy's long-run growth potential has been lifted permanently from the meagre pre- Covid levels. The jury is still out, but the continued lacklustre productivity growth over the past few years limits the enthusiasm, in our view. While potential growth may not fall back to below 0.5%, as was the case during 2000-20, recent OECD analysis projects it to be less than 1% and hence below the Eurozone average. Economists also generally view low and stable inflation as preferable to deflation. The latter can have pernicious and difficult-to-reverse effects on demand, as it creates incentives to delay consumption. A 2% target is viewed as far enough away from zero to create a buffer from deflation even during economic downturns. Then why not target 3%, or more? Because when inflation is low, it tends to be less volatile. And with low and steady inflation, it becomes rational for consumers to not spend too much time worrying about prices. This “rational inattention” is desirable from central bankers’ perspective.

records.text: The Leadership Transition We do not expect any major institutional changes at Chairman Warsh’s first meeting. But questions could come up in the press conference about whether he plans to act on his past criticisms of the Fed on themes including communications practices, balance sheet policy, and financial regulation. On communications practices, Warsh has called for saying less, and many investors have wondered if he might move to cancel the Summary of Economic Projections. While we do see some potential areas for improvement, we do not expect any major near-term changes. The FOMC just had a lengthy discussion of its communication practices last year in its framework review and was unable to agree on any changes. In addition, because making the reaction function more transparent should itself support macroeconomic stabilization, we think it would be hard to justify moving in the opposite direction. On the balance sheet, regulatory and supervisory changes are likely to have some impact on banks’ demand for reserves balances and ultimately on the size of the balance sheet. But as we explained in greater depth in March, we do not expect the FOMC to shrink the balance sheet more substantially. On financial regulatory policy, Warsh has argued for a lighter touch on small- and medium-sized banks in particular. records.text: 2 Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 Overview & legal framework In 1997, the Diet passed a revised Bank of Japan Act, marking the first comprehensive revision of the BoJ’s governing statute since 1942. The reform reflected three forces: the discrediting of the MoF-led framework after the bubble collapse, political damage to the MoF from a series of scandals in the mid-1990s, and a global shift toward statutory central bank independence. The reform removed the MoF’s supervisory authority over monetary policy, made the Policy Board the decision-maker for monetary policy through the MPM process, granted officers five-year terms with dismissal limited to narrow grounds, and required the publication of minutes and reporting to the Diet. The new Act took effect on 1 April 1998. The 2% inflation target was adopted in 2013 The BoJ has one monetary policy objective: price stability. Financial system stability is also part of its mandate, but it reflects its role as bankers’ bank and lender of last resort rather than an objective of monetary policy itself. The Act does not define a numerical inflation target or an operational measure of price stability. The current 2% target was introduced through a sequence of policy steps rather than specified in the Act. In March 2006, under Governor Fukui, the BoJ introduced its “Understanding of Medium- to Long-Term Price Stability” (中長期的な物価安定の理解). A prolonged disruption from here could further support EV sales, but we also see a risk that the conflict prompts a global standstill in auto purchases as higher energy prices dent economic growth. records.text: Marvin Loh, Cayla Seder June 15, 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material FOMC preview: the Warsh era begins Kevin Warsh will take the podium on Wednesday in his first presser as Chairman of the FOMC. There will not be any rates or balance sheet announcements at this meeting, although we should start to see how Warsh intends to drive changes at the Fed. The policy statement, SEP and dots may very well lean moderately hawkishly, with higher inflation potentially moving the 2026 median dot to unchanged. The long run dot will nonetheless be below current levels, so the message will remain that cuts are appro priate at some time in the future. The balance sheet may also get a bit more attention at this meeting, as Warsh has advocated a smaller footprint, although we don’t think there is much scope for any major alternations to in reserve management policy in the foreseeable future. Outside of policy, Warsh may start to alter the communication process by limiting economic and funds projections, shorten and possibly red ucing pressers, while limiting the board’s approach to Fed speak. So, while there may not be any policy announcements over the next few meetings, the groundwork for changing Fed communications is likely to start at this meeting. records.text: ernment’s economic policy 9-member MPC; Governor, internal and 4 external members (appointed by Chancellor); Governor serves an 8-year term Source: BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Voting rules and membership structure The BoJ decides policy at Monetary Policy Meetings (MPMs) based on a majority vote of the Policy Board. The Board has nine members: the Governor, two Deputy Governors, and six other members. All are appointed by the Cabinet with the consent of both Houses of the Diet. They serve renewable five‑year terms, with expiration dates staggered across members. Each member has one vote, and the Chairperson decides in the event of a tie. The Governor normally serves as Chairperson; if the Chairperson is unable to attend a meeting, a previously designated Board member performs the Chairperson’s duties. In practice, the Governor and two Deputy Governors form the core policy line, and splits among them in the formal vote are extremely rare. MPMs are held, in principle, eight times a year and run over two days. The first day is spent reviewing economic and financial conditions in Japan and abroad based on staff reports. The second day is devoted to debate and the policy decision. Unlike the Fed or ECB, the BoJ does not pre‑announce the release time of its decision. The policy statement is released immediately after deliberations conclude on MPM day 2, typically between 11:30 and 13:00 JST. records.text: The zero rate cycle – financial crisis to pandemic (2009-2022) This favourable regime was starkly and abruptly disrupted by the Global Financial Crisis of 2008/9. The economic consequences of this crash were so severe that it heralded a period of unprecedented monetary support. Strikingly, the economic recovery from the financial crisis was weaker than the average recovery since 1950 (Exhibit 6). records.text: Factors impacting post-IPO performance Hong Kong IPOs throughout the 2025-26 cycle have demonstrated remarkably post-listing performance. On average, newly listed companies since 2025 delivered a 45% return on their first trading day, expanding to 49% in the first month, and reaching 67% within three months post-listing. However, post-IPO performance dispersion remains high, characterized by extreme outliers; the top-performing stock rallied more than tenfold within six months of its IPO, whereas the worst-performing one declined by 74%. A granular analysis of issuer characteristics reveals several key structural drivers of these return differentials: Market Capitalization and Listing Type: Large-cap listings tend to generate n superior post-IPO returns, whereas dual-listed companies underperform compared to those executing a fresh, standalone listing in Hong Kong. Cornerstone Backing: A moderate cornerstone shareholder ownership, specifically n within the 30% to 50% range, serves as an indicator of potential long-term outperformance. However, excessive concentration that severely restricts the tradable free float can negatively impact post-IPO liquidity and performance. Retail Demand: Stocks exhibiting high oversubscription ratios tend to demonstrate n stronger price appreciation, particularly during the first week of trading. Moreover, consumer spending has so far held up reasonably well on both sides of the Atlantic since the start of the conflict. While these are both welcome developments for the growth outlook, we see three reasons why it is too early for complacency on real income and consumer spending in the coming months. First, while gasoline prices jumped shortly after the start of the war (and may n ease following the recent interim deal), the passthrough from wholesale gas and electricity prices to consumers is more drawn out. Second, seasonal spending patterns should amplify the hit to income this winter when energy demand peaks, especially in Europe. Lastly, while outsized tax refunds dampened the real income hit in the US this spring, this temporary boost is now behind us and we expect real cash flow to stagnate on a year-on-year basis in H2. records.text: Lower tariffs and rising globalization There was a concerted shift towards lower trade tariffs, which, together with the ending of many capital controls, boosted world trade growth and spurred economic integration (Exhibit 3). The 1986 Uruguay Round of GATT was more comprehensive than anything that had come before. It included services and capital as well as textiles and agriculture and was the firs t time that developing countries played an active role in trade negotiations. This marked the start of a new era of globalisation that expanded rapidly following the collapse of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the signing of NAFTA in 1994, India joining the WTO in 1995, and, finally , China joining in 2001. Between 1995 and 2010, the pace of world trade growth grew at twice the pace of World GDP . The outsourcing of manufacturing to lower-cost regions of the world boosted world trade and profit shares of GDP and the cost of importing capital goods back to the West dropped dramatically. Previously, we had projected the Fed would stay on hold through 2026, with hikes only likely if the unemployment rate fell below 4% or long-term inflation expectations showed evidence of becoming de-anchored. We think strong growth, a gradually tightening labor market and persistently high inflation should prompt three consecutive moves starting in December (i.e., after the midterm elections), with the aim of withdrawing the monetary stimulus provided by last year's three ‘insurance’ cuts. We note that an earlier start may be possible depending on the course of the Middle East conflict and the labor market's trajectory. records.text: US Daily Data Recap15 June 2026 ab 2 First June manufacturing survey moderates, but still in expansion The FRB of New York Empire State manufacturing general business conditions index fell 13.9 points to 5.7 in June, partially unwinding improvements in the past two months. Adjusted to ISM weights, the index fell 4.6 points to 53.4. The new orders and shipments indexes both retraced April and May improvement in June. The new orders index fell a sharp 19.2 points to 3.5, and the shipments index, which can be more volatile, fell 10.3 points to 8.6. Despite the deterioration in some details, the headline index and nearly all subcomponents, except for inventories and supply availability, are currently in expansion territory. In June, the inventories index fell 9.7 points to 0.0, and the supply availability index, which fell 3.2 points to -13.9. The supply availability index has been in contraction since December 2024. In other details, the employment index edged up 1.3 points to 9.6, a high since December 2022, while the average workweek index fell 6.4 points to 5.1. The delivery times index fell 8.5 points to 11.9 but remained somewhat elevated. Survey responses were collected between June 2 and June 9, a period that saw some moderation in Brent crude oil prices, as we noted in our preview (link here). Price indexes in the Empire State survey climbed since the beginning of the Middle East conflict, but both edged down slightly in June. The prices paid index fell 1.6 points to 61.

For economies and equity markets, the key drivers were: Low valuations and disinflation The start of this super cycle followed the bruising de-rating and poor returns of financial assets driven by the combination of high infla tion and rising rates in the 1970s. At the end of the decade, the so-called Volcker credit crunch had pushed policy rates in the US from around 10% to close to 20%, triggering a recession and a deep bear market; valuations collapsed and the S&P 500 reached a trough trailing P/E of 7x. As infla tion reached a peak, and interest rates began to moderate, equity and bond markets staged a major recovery. Supply side reforms and lower taxes In combination with easing inflationary pressures and lower interest rates, sweeping economic reforms began to emerge. The Reagan and Thatcher ‘revolutions’ resulted in waves of deregulation, lower unionisation, privatisation, lower taxes and the end of credit controls (Exhibit 1 ). Eventually, many other countries followed suit, supporting a broader economic recovery. Lower macro volatility The combination of these factors resulted in a healthier mix between growth and infla tion as well as an era of lower volatility in macro variables (Exhibit 2 ). A list of key BoC tools is displayed in Exhibit 14. To keep CORRA within the target range the BoC relies on a floor system. Within a 30bp operating band, the policy target is set 5bp above the bottom of the band (Exhibit 13). To keep CORRA from falling below the operating band, the BoC sets the floor using the overnight reverse repo rate (ORR, equal to policy rate target) and deposit rate (equal to bottom of the band, 5bp below policy target). The BoC’s deposit rate is currently set 5bps below the target rate to help CORRA print closer to target by improving the circulation of settlement balances (encourages banks to lend in repo at rates above the deposit rate, which operates as a floor). The overnight reverse repo operations were used to temporarily withdraw liquidity from the system to help reinforce the target rate. In 2023, once liquidity had been sufficiently drained via QT and repo rates were not at risk of falling below the operating band, the BoC shifted from daily to ad-hoc ORR operations. records.text: US Viewpoint | 14 June 2026 9 Market pricing: FF & SOFR indicators We review key means by which to evaluate Fed pricing across FOMC OIS, fed funds futures, & SOFR futures. Our preferred means is to use FOMC OIS, which we believe is the cleanest read of Fed expectations. FOMC OIS: cleanest read of Fed expectations FOMC OIS are the simplest instrument to look at near-term Fed expectations. FOMC OIS are OTC swaps that cover the period of one FOMC meeting to the next. The OIS fixed rate is the daily fed funds effective rate reported by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FRBNY) between two FOMC meetings. The contract reference period starts the day after a scheduled FOMC statement release & ends on the day of the next meeting statement release. FOMC OIS contracts are typically only liquid out 6M to 1Y max. For example, the July ’26 FOMC statement is expected to be released on July 29 & the September ’26 FOMC statement is expected to be released on September 16. The July FOMC OIS contract will reference the daily average effective federal funds rate from July 30 through September 16.
