Inflation is measured using the CPI, but the BoC’s preferred inflation measures are the CPI-trim and CPI-median to filter out short-term volatility and assess underlying trends. Thus, while setting monetary policy the bank looks through temporary movements and focuses on core inflation measures. The flexible exchange rate enables the BoC to carry out an independent monetary policy aligned with domestic conditions and the inflation target, while also helping the economy adjust to external and internal shocks. Within this framework and given uncertainty around the level of economic slack and maximum sustainable employment, the BoC considers a broad range of indicators when setting policy. Monetary policy is primarily implemented through adjustments to short-term interest rates – the overnight rate, the bank rate and the deposit rate – with the overnight rate being the key instrument. Moreover, they are supported by additional tools when rates are very low, such as quantitative easing (QE). QE was used during the COVID-19 pandemic to support the economy while the overnight rate was at 0.25%. These measures influence demand through their effects on interest rates, asset prices, and the exchange rate. Since policy actions take time to affect the economy, decisions are forward-looking and depend on the balance between demand and productive capacity. Instead of reconsidering the 2% target itself, the current review is focused on how the framework operates in an environment increasingly shaped by supply-side shocks and structural changes. Recent years have highlighted the importance of factors such as supply chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions, changes in global trade patterns, demographic trends, and climate-related events. These forces can create trade-offs for monetary policy, including situations where inflation rises alongside weak growth. The ongoing review therefore aims to assess whether the existing flexible inflation-targeting framework is sufficiently equipped to respond to these challenges, rather than altering its core objective. The review is also reassessing how the BoC measures underlying inflation, as new and persistent shocks hit the economy, such as trade disruptions. The BoC is evaluating the performance of its existing core measures—CPI‑ trim and CPI‑median— acknowledging their limitations during shocks. This includes examining how certain components, such as mortgage interest costs, may distort signals and complicate real‑time assessment. In parallel, the BoC is exploring refinements to these measures, as well as potential additions, such as multivariate core trend inflation and artificial intelligence with a clustering algorithm technique

records.text: 14 Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 Securities Lending Facility (SLF) The BoJ’s Securities Lending Facility (SLF) functions as a repo transaction between the BoJ and domestic financial institutions, such as commercial banks and investment banks. The BoJ describes the facility as a tool that provides a temporary and secondary source of JGBs to the market, with a view to facilitating the Bank’s money market operations and contributing to the smooth settlement of both JGBs and funds. • Eligible securities: Japanese government bonds with coupons and T-bills held by the BoJ. Issues sold through the Securities Lending Facility are listed on the BoJ’s website. While the cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) issue for JGB futures tends to attract the highest amount of successful bids, other JGBs— including 2-year, 5-year, 20- year, 30-year, and 40-year issues— are also sold through the SLF. • Repurchase conditions: The SLF is designed to temporarily provide JGBs held by the BoJ to the market, with each issue sold on the condition that it will subsequently be repurchased. Repurchases occur on the next trading day after the sale, but rollovers can be requested up to 21 times for each issue. For market stability, the maximum consecutive usage period for JGBs will be set at 30 business days starting July 16, 2026. • Frequency of use: The Securities Lending Facility was utilized 501 times in FY2023 and 488 times in both FY2024 and FY2025, and continues to be used. We cover the Fed’s dual mandate, voting rules & membership structure, the communication toolkit, frameworks to assess the policy stance, market pricing (using fed funds & SOFR) and the balance sheet. Dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices The Fed has a dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices, which it has defined as a 2% PCE inflation target. The dual mandate can lead to trade-offs in the short run. Rate hikes tend to lower inflation and raise unemployment, while cuts do the opposite. The trade-off gets challenging when the economy is hit by supply shocks. In these instances, addressing risks to one mandate means exacerbating risks to the other. Fed voting rules: it takes seven The Fed sets policy based on a majority vote by the FOMC. There are up to 12 voting members on the FOMC: all Governors, the NY Fed President and four regional Presidents who rotate annually. So it usually takes seven votes to get a majority. records.text: Europe Developed Markets 15 June 2026 Citi Research 2 Riksbank: On Hold Now and Later The Riksbank continues to be in a much more comfortable position, less of a conundrum, than many of its peers in advanced economies in the face of the oil shock. The extremely weak inflation prints since the start of the year and evidence of low resource utilization in the labour market allow ample room for looking through the energy shock. Ex-energy CPI inflation in the past three months has printed on average 50bp below the March MPR forecast, which will likely result into a likely down-revision of the Riksbank June MPR inflation forecasts. A VAT rate cut on foodstuff is reducing inflation at the moment (food CPI inflation was -4.7% YY in May), and government interventions are helping to contain the oil pass-through. But even ex-food and energy inflation has been weakening since January – Eurostat’s HICP-measured core inflation (ex-food and energy) in Sweden stood at 1.2% YY in May, up from 0.5% YY in April, according to our estimates. T o be sure, underlying price pressures may not stay as soft as the latest CPI numbers suggest ex-energy CPIF at just 0.5% YY in May, and most Riksbank’s underlying inflation measures ranging between 1% and 2% (see Fig 1). In the May meeting, the BoK raised both growth and inflation forecasts, attributing the changes to robust semiconductor exports, higher global energy prices and rising demand-side inflationary pressure. Governor Hyun- Song Shin adopted a hawkish tone in the post-meeting press conference. He said that MPB members were broadly aligned on the direction of the policy rate and that trade-off from hiking rates was limited, given stronger growth, higher inflation and lingering financial stability risks. On FX, he suggested a narrow South Korea–US rates gap could help stabilize the KRW in the long run. May inflation spiked to 3.1% y/y from 2.6% in April, which explains Governor Shin’s hawkish comments, in our view. While we expect inflation to remain close to the current level in the coming months, we think the BoK will keep a cautious tone to ensure price pressures do not spread. We forecast year-on-year inflation to peak in H2. Exports stayed robust: container throughput at major ports averaged 6.6 million TEU in May, matching the average for the first four months, and year-on-year shipments to the US should climb beyond April’s 11.3% thanks to a favorable base effect. By contrast, domestic consumption has stayed weak, largely because subsidies have been scaled back. The gap between the CPI and the PPI might also widen. We expect May’s headline PPI inflation to have accelerated from 2.8% y/y in April, driven by higher metal and coal prices despite monthly declines in oil and chemicals. CPI inflation should have stayed modest, as pork, vegetable and domestic fuel prices fell month-on- month and the PPI pass-through remains limited. Demand-side weakness seems to be policy-driven, especially from reduced consumer-goods trade-in subsidies and an ongoing anti-involution campaign, so policymakers will likely finetune existing measures rather than introduce fresh stimulus. Even if May’s growth stays below the GDP target’s 4.5% lower bound, we expect their response to be faster bond issuance and fiscal spending rather than policy rate cuts, given that banks’ net interest margin remains low at 1.4% in Q1 (see China: Slower growth in April amid policy headwinds, dated 18 May). records.text: 1 Insights Market Narratives in Focus: Too many worries to matter16 Jun 2026Equities. We wouldn’t blame investors for feeling bruised after an “eventful” first half of 2026. Our Narrative Map currentlyflags half a dozen market threats—from AI and crowded trades to inflation, rates, liquidity, and debt levels (Figure 1). Anyone of these could have derailed equity returns YTD. Paradoxically, their coexistence may be a source of resilience. Whenrisks are numerous, none dominates. Our Systemic Risk Index—tracking the breadth of drivers behind market volatility—points to exactly that: since Liberation Day, the influence of key market drivers has declined steadily and now sits near a30-year low (Figure 2). That matters. Sharp drawdowns tend to occur when risk is concentrated—not dispersed. Today’sbackdrop suggests the opposite. Despite a crowded risk narrative, investors continue to run meaningful exposure to riskyassets. For now, dispersion of media and market narratives is doing the heavy lifting—creating a more stable backdropand extending the runway for risk assets. In other words, plenty to fear, but not enough to panic. Perhaps when investorshave too much to worry about, they don’t worry too much.FX. We still project EURNOK sliding to 10.8 and EURSEK to 10.7 by year end, albeit now with less scope for upside versus the USD given our EURUSD view. Norway has benefited considerably this year as a net energy exporter, but we think this source of upside is mostly in the price, as FX transactions by the Norges Bank tend to limit the impact on the NOK of elevated energy prices. Norway’s net energy trade balance was worth 21% of GDP in 2024, the highest in the G10. Energy supply is unlikely to normalise immediately, even if the Strait of Hormuz reopens fully, so we expect prices to remain elevated for some time. However, this boost to the national energy industry reduces the central bank’s need to buy NOK to fund the budget deficit (Figure 1). The resulting impact on NOK flows is more muted and limits the supportive impact of energy price shocks. Additionally, we expect the Norges Bank to remain hawkish and the currency to retain a yield buffer versus peers. We attribute the sizable outflows to three factors: 1) Elevated volatility and strong returns that prompted foreign investors to prudently book profits; 2) Risk-limit constraints on single-country exposure, forcing a reduction in Korean positions; 3) Tech sector rotation from cyclical to more growth-oriented themes, as investors rebalance away from cyclical stocks (see page 4 in KRW: Navigating the Flows, dated 15 May). In Taiwan foreign ownership of Taiwan equities has reached a historic high (47.5% as of end-May) and foreigners have generated 5x return on Taiwan equities (Figure x). These stellar returns naturally prompt some profit-taking but in spite of this net foreign flows have been largely flat, in contrast to Korea. We believe the relative under-performance versus the KOSPI has helped attract recent inflows, as Taiwan equities have more consistent and stable earnings-growth profile. Domestic retail investors: There is a notable pattern across the Asian current account surplus economies of retail investors becoming more active in foreign equites since 2024. We think this investor cohort is particularly sensitive to historic returns though - this appears most evident in Korea, where Kospi outperformance this year appears to caused retail investors to pivot to domestic equities and effectively halt foreign equity buying.

records.text: : Media keeps on the pressure Source: State Street Markets, MKT MediaStats, Bloomberg Statement neutrality: The policy statement is likely to be tweaked in the manner that the hawkish dissenters wanted to see at the last meeting. Recall that Logan, Kashkari and Hammack objected to the dovish policy bias from the continued use of “the extent and timing of additional adjustments” statement. With inflation trending higher and data getting stronger since the last meeting, this phrase will likely be removed, implying 2-way risk to the next policy move. This view was affirmed by Waller a few weeks ago when he stated that elevated inflation no longer justified the easing bias. That said, we think that near-term EGB issuance could lead to some modest widening of sovereign rates versus swap rates as EGB issuance is running slightly below its 3y average. We went short 2y Italy after the Iran conflict erupted but closed the short at 2.75%. Some clients have asked us if Italy is more vulnerable than France. We think that Italy may eventually underperform France if Italian budget data disappoints, with the 2027 budget discussion a likely focal point, but we do not see the case for material underperformance in the next two months as a moderate search for carry in EGBs has resumed (see also this note).

Taken together, the balance of signals from our model points to a meaningful hawkish shift in President Lagarde communication, characterized by stronger inflation concerns and a reduced emphasis on growth and labor market risks. records.text: Qualitative Monetary Easing (QQE), the balance sheet itself was positioned as a primary policy tool, with the monetary base serving as the operating target. Within this framework, large-scale asset purchases were actively conducted to achieve that target. However, following the end of QQE and YCC in March 2024, the BoJ reverted to a framework centered on short-term interest rates, with the uncollateralized overnight call rate as its policy target. Under this framework, the balance sheet is no longer treated as a primary policy objective, and balance sheet-related tools—such as JGB purchases —are used only as operational measures to support market functioning and JGB market stability. In other words, these measures do not serve as signals for changes in the policy rate.

records.text: Global Strategy15 June 2026 ab 16 'Challenging': Periods of peak momentum and elevated valuations are typically followed by valuation compression Despite near record economic uncertainty, ranging from inflation and geopolitics to sovereign debt concerns, markets appear largely insensitive to negative news. One illustration of this disconnect is the divergence between a near record low VIX and a near record high Economic Uncertainty Index (40% monthly correlation between the two series since 1995). Historically, such phases of “irrational exuberance” can persist for extended periods. During the dot-com bubble, momentum outperformance lasted for around 20 months, even as relative valuations reached new extremes. A similar dynamic played out between November 2024 and February 2026, before valuations began to gradually re-rate. The question now is whether further re-rating lies ahead. Though skeptical of forward guidance, Warsh could have attempted to counterbalance the hawkish signal from the SEP , and it was significant that he did not distance himself from that view. While he noted the Fed has little ability to combat inflation that arises from supply shocks, he also emphasized that the Fed has an important role in preventing those supply shocks from broadening out inflation via “second and third -order effects.” He also did not lean on any of the potential dovish arguments he has referenced in the past, e.g., the disinflationary forces from AI and productivity or the more benign signals from alternative measures of trend inflation, like trimmed mean. Indeed, Warsh repeated several times the importance of the Fed delivering on its “price stability” mandate, which he mentioned a dozen times. The closest Warsh came to forward guidance was “So what you heard from the Committee today is we've got some work to be done on the price stability front. “ He also noted that “we'll be meeting again in six weeks. TONA also serves as the yen risk-free rate, replacing JPY LIBOR and acting as the benchmark for the floating leg in a range of transactions, including swaps. As such, the BoJ’s control of the overnight rate anchors pricing across the yen rates curve. How the BoJ controls the overnight rate The BoJ sets both a floor and a ceiling rate and conducts market operations to keep the uncollateralized overnight rate close to this range. The floor is the interest rate paid on excess reserves through the complementary deposit facility. This rate is set equal to the target for the uncollateralized overnight call rate (currently 1%). The ceiling is the basic loan rate under the complementary lending facility, currently 1.25%, at which eligible institutions can borrow overnight from the BoJ against collateral. TONA tends to trade slightly below the IOER. records.text: The Post Modern Cycle – Navigating the Capex Boom In our 2022 Global Strategy Paper, The Post Modern Cycle; Positioning for Secular Change, we focused on a series of emerging structural changes that we argued would drive a differ ent set of challenges and opportunities for investors compared with previous cycles. We described the period post WWII through to the late 1970s as the ‘Traditional’ cycle, which was characterised by high volatility in macro variables. The 1980s saw the emergence of what we describe as the ‘Modern’ cycle, dominated by low infla tion and macro volatility coupled with the effec ts of globalisation. The ‘Post Modern’ cycle refers to the period post the pandemic when dramatic changes began to occur in economies, geopolitics and technology. The traditional investment cycle (pre 1980s) was generally short and volatilen reflecting booms and busts and periods of high and low inflation and interest rates; investors typically required a high dividend yield to compensate for the risks in equity markets. The ‘Modern’ cycle (from the early 1980s) was characterised by more stability andn predictability. It benefited from sustained falls in inflation, interest rates and risk premia. Geopolitical tensions eased and supply side reforms accompanied waves of deregulation, the end of capital controls, deeper capital markets and stronger world trade growth. In this note, we ask whether the performance this decade is "as good as its gets" for Italy or whether it marks a durable improvement in economic performance. We show that the Italian outperformance in recent years has largely been driven by expansionary fiscal policy: a very generous construction incentive − which eventually proved to be too expensive for the Italian budget and had to be discontinued − and the EU's large NGEU RRF facility, where the last disbursements are set to happen this year. The spending of the NGEU funds may continue in 2027, but will eventually fade. At that stage, the Italian outperformance might well come to an end. Hence, current macro conditions may indeed be "as good as it gets". However, in our view, marked fiscal tightening is not expected until 2028 and there is a chance that Italy's potential growth rate has improved somewhat relative to the prior two decades, implying that the cyclical growth slowdown may be moderate rather than disruptive. Nevertheless, we do acknowledge clear improvement, above all greater political stability. The next parliamentary elections have to be held only by December 2027. The BoJ’s role in FX intervention The authority to conduct FX intervention rests with the Minister of Finance, and exchange rate policy is set outside the monetary policy framework. records.text: European Equity Strategy15 June 2026 ab 5 European Equity Strategy UBS Research Earnings in focus Earnings remain the key transmission channel for European equity performance, particularly in a market structure increasingly driven by shorter-term, hedge fund-led pricing dynamics that react quickly to earnings news and revisions. Consistent with this, Figure 5 below shows that earnings revisions have delivered strong alpha in Europe over the last 20 years, reinforcing the importance of momentum-style signals. However, our analysis suggests that relying solely on consensus-driven revisions risks missing turning points – especially on the downside. The UBS Machine Learning earnings model provides a complementary and often more forward-looking signal, with particular efficacy in downgrade cycles where analysts tend to adjust forecasts too slowly. When backt-tested, this too can be used to generate a Sharpe ratio of around 1x ex transaction costs. The ML/consensus gap is especially valuable today, as the macro backdrop shifts toward slower growth and margin pressure for many European companies. records.text: M Idea 2 June FOMC Takeaways: A hawkish shift, less communication, reformist The Press Conference: Hawkish and Inflation-Focused The Press Conference was hawkish, like the statement. Chairman Warsh emphasized that “we have the capability and commitment to deliver on our price stability objective of 2%. That's what we're going to do.” He repeated the idea: “this committee unambiguously and unanimously have decided we are going to deliver” on its inflation target. And before the Q and A period, he emphasized inflation above target "[t]hat's been going on for more than five years. " "I've said for years inflation is a choice. You bet it is." The SEP showed a sharp increase in the core inflation estimate for this year. Chair Warsh downplayed it. "There's a range of questions on first and second-round effects" driving oil price increase into core inflation. Rather he was more focused on the above-target trend in inflation. Referring to the FOMC that submitted forecasts this meeting, he said: "They didn't feel bound by them six weeks from now or six days from now. " His press conference had a hawkish enough tone that he was asked “one might wonder why you didn’t raise rates today….” To which Chair Warsh replied that “I've got nothing more to say than the statement itself.” On the labor market, there was no mention of downside risks. LLC US Daily: June FOMC Recap: Hikes Look More Likely but Are Still Not Our Base Case 17 June 2026 | 7:58PM EDT The June FOMC meeting delivered a hawkish surprise, with nine participants n projecting a hike in 2026 (vs. our expectation of three) and the median projection for 2027 Q4/Q4 core PCE inflation rising to 2.5% (vs. our expectation of 2.3%). Market pricing for the fed funds rate at the end of 2026 rose by 20bp in response to the projections and Chairman Kevin Warsh’s press conference. Today’s meeting raises the risk of interest rate hikes later this year, but our base n case is still that the FOMC will leave the policy rate unchanged this year. A majority could support a hike, perhaps for a range of different reasons, if upcoming inflation prints are uncomfortable and job growth remains solid. But we suspect that most of the voters still lean toward an unchanged policy rate and that participants treated the news about a deal with Iran and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz cautiously for now. If so, today’s projections could prove stale if trade resumes, which should resolve the most serious source of upside risk to inflation fairly quickly. The Statement and SEP also signaled a shift toward less guidance from FOMC. The statement itself was sharply truncated. It dropped the language providing any sort of forward guidance. The statement reflected a unanimous vote, and might imply a change in communication strategy looking ahead. The path of the funds rate will depend on incoming economic data and the FOMC’s reaction function. It also assesses financial conditions to judge how the policy stance is transmitting to the economy. Together, these inform whether the current policy stance remains appropriate. Communication and where the signal sits The BoJ’s policy signal is concentrated in a relatively small set of MPM-related outputs: the policy statement, Governor press conference, Outlook Report, Summary of Opinions, and minutes. The statement and press conference carry the near-term policy signal, while the Outlook Report and Summary of Opinions help markets read the Board’s assessment of inflation, risks, and the policy path. Speeches can be used to shape the policy narrative or prepare the ground for policy shifts, while staff research provides context on the analytical lenses the Bank wants markets to use. Policy rate, balance sheet, and operations Following the exit from yield curve control in 2024, the BoJ has returned to a rate-based framework, with the uncollateralized overnight call rate as the policy target. records.text: MPMs. Initially introduced in October 2000, the Outlook Report contains the Board’s median forecasts for real GDP and CPI over the current and next two fiscal years, the range of individual member projections, a detailed assessment of the baseline scenario for the economic and price outlook, an assessment of the risks to that outlook, and the Board’s thinking on future policy conduct. It is the BoJ’s closest counterpart to the Fed’s SEP, though the projections do not include a policy rate forecast. The published material consists of the short “Bank’s View” released alongside the MPM decision, followed by the full report at 14:00 JST on the next business day. The Outlook Report generates less immediate market reaction than the policy statement and the Governor’s post‑MPM press conference, but it is central to reading the medium- term policy path because it sets out the baseline forecasts, the risks around them, and the policy-relevant conditions to monitor. As a result, the policy path should be read as conditional on the projections and the risks around them. Tracking how incoming data and Board communication evolve relative to the Outlook Report, particularly on the inflation outlook and the wage‑price dynamic, is key to assessing where policy is heading. The volume of output has increased under Governor Ueda, alongside a greater emphasis on analytical framing. Attribution and form matter. Work associated with the Monetary Affairs Department often sets out the policy-relevant issues and analytical lenses the Bank wants markets to use. Department-attributed work carries the strongest institutional signal. When such analysis is published in a more accessible format, such as BoJ Review, it should be read as flagging policy questions the Bank considers especially important.

However, following the March 2024 Monetary Policy Meeting—at which the BoJ decided to abolish yield curve control (YCC) and remove the overshooting commitment—the fixed-rate method is no longer employed. Consequently, JGB purchases are currently conducted via the competitive auction method, namely Rinban operations. Under this framework, the BoJ accepts bids starting with the highest yield (lowest price), followed by the second highest, and so on. Each Rinban operation is conducted as a multiple-price competitive auction in which counterparties bid “desired yield spreads,” defined as the difference between “benchmark yields” (the previous trading day’s closing values based on the JSDA’s Reference Statistical Prices (Yields) for OTC Bond Transactions) and the yields at which counterparties seek to sell to the Bank. The BoJ makes offers for coupon-bearing JGBs by residual maturity. • Purchase amounts and schedule: At each quarter end, the BoJ publishes the purchase size per operation and the planned monthly frequency of operations for each residual maturity bucket over the coming quarter. But the pressure on software is staying localized, because 1) the rating agencies are still net upgrading spec-grade software names & 2) private credit software loan markdowns are very modest, with hardly any dispersion being priced. Hedge ratios in Japan have steadily fallen over the past decade and we don’t expect a change in trajectory in the coming months. South Korean institutions remain large buyers of foreign assets, more so among the pension fund community. However, the National Pension Service (NPS) has taken steps to reduce its FX footprint this year. It has announced a temporary waiver on portfolio rebalancing (to limit KOSPI selling in light of its sharp gains) and raised the ceiling on FX hedging by 5pp to 20% (15% strategic + 5% tactical). This year, we estimated index days based on 2015, and this methodology has proven accurate thus far. It suggests prices are likely to have been sampled on June 9th. However, the publication date is quite late in July - the 22nd - which suggests the ONS would allow for quite a wide gap between prices being sampled and published. We had seen such a wide gap once this year - with the December data published in January - and publication days have skewed later in the month this year. We, thus, assume that prices will be collected on the 9th. We assume a modest 0.3%M pick up in food prices, with core goods prices flat on the month. We think there was still decent spring season clothes discounting in the first half of June, although we do think that a later index day would spell a weaker core goods inflation print. Due to diesel prices, auto fuels look to have fallen by another 0.5%M; heating fuel is due to fall by 15%M again, we think. Services-wise, we see stronger air fares with a later index day. records.text: ab 15 June 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives Italy: As good as it gets − or the new normal? What a difference a decade makes... We recently downgraded our GDP growth forecast for Italy this year (-0.4pp to 0.5%) amidst the energy crisis. However, in this note, we take a broader perspective and assess Italy's macro performance on a longer horizon. One of the notable − and often underappreciated − developments in the Eurozone this decade so far has been the economic outperformance of Italy − both relative to peers and relative to Italy's own past. Since 2019, Italian real GDP growth has exceeded the Eurozone average, Germany and France; unemployment has fallen faster; and long-standing north-south disparities in Italy have narrowed somewhat. Corporate leverage has declined steadily and is now lower than in other large EU countries. Italy's net international investment position turned positive in 2020 for the first time since the mid-1980s. The political environment has also been more stable than in prior decades, judged by the number of governments and the relative stability of opinion polls. Reflecting this improved macro and political backdrop, the BTP-Bund spread has averaged well below past-decade norms and has peaked at much lower levels during market stress. ...but how long will it last? records.text: TRADE IDEA T R A D E I D E A 16/06/2026 1 EM rates: Extending target on HUF 5y receiver We extend the target on our M26 5y HUF receiver to 4.50%, from 4.90%, which we initiated in EM rates: The case for HUF receivers, dated 20 April. Since entry, continued softness in Hungary’s inflation picture and a lower country risk premium have driven the belly of the HUF curve around 90bp richer. We also trail the stop 60bp lower to 5.80%. We continue to like the disinflationary story in Hungary both from a cyclical (Figure 1) and structural perspective. Cyclically, we have had soft January repricings and the soft underlying inflation trend has continued so far, suggesting that inflation should remain within the NBH inflation target range throughout the forecast horizon. Consumer inflation expectations, as evidenced by Eurostat data, have also remained well-anchored and have meaningfully diverged from CE3 peers (Figure 2). Structurally, increased investment driven by FDI inflows and accelerating EU fund absorption can durably lift productivity and ease the persistent upward pressure on unit labour costs that has been a key source of services stickiness. The narrative around euro adoption should also provide a macro anchor that over time allows HUF rates to converge towards levels seen in Poland and the Czech Republic (see Hungary: Euro vision, dated 4 June). For the moment, the greater risk is reaching the 2% inflation goal, which Warsh emphasized over the employment situation. The task forces that he is forming may prove a way to implement drastic and possibly damaging institutional changes, although we did not get that sense at this meeting. Instead, communications are likely to change. Our view is that pressers may go back to a quarterly cadence, while the SEP will tie dots to economic regimes, which we feel the Fed has discussed in the past. Although Chairman Warsh did not provide clarity on how exactly Fed communication style will change, he made clear all forms of communication are subject for review. Since the days of Covid, the magnitude of Fed speak has increased notably. In 2025 Fed members hit the wires 115 times, nearly double the 10y average of 69 times. Nonetheless, volatility around rate expectations indicates all that talk was not cheap, as volatility generally eased as Fed speak increased. This is notable given the elevated degree of macroeconomic uncertainty in recent years (Figure 4). Without the talk, it would not be surprising to see more volatility around rate expectations as markets navigate data with less influence from Fed speakers. Tensions have flared at times, but dated Brent prices and crack spreads have still fallen back from their April peaks. Temporary oil buffers, such as lower levels of Chinese imports, floating inventories and stockpile draws continue to cushion the market from the supply shock. If Strait-of-Hormuz flows resume in June, we think Brent could dip to around USD70/bbl before recovering. However, if the conflict persists into August, USD140/bbl looks possible, with physical shortages becoming more pressing as inventories are depleted and seasonal demand increases during the summer. At this point, significant demand destruction would be likely. Should the conflict escalate even further, and continue into Q4, oil prices may peak at USD200/bbl, in our view. Warmer weather in Asia may lead to strong gas demand (perhaps amplified by El Niño), intensifying competition with Europe during its storage-fill season. This discrepancy suggests that the BoC will likely continue to grow its asset purchases or repo operations, especially as additional GoC coupon securities mature and roll off from their holdings. Notably, BoC repo operations have experienced more significant growth compared to T- bill purchases, which have fallen short of expectations. The underperformance in T-bill purchases can be attributed to low liquidity in the T-bill market, which restricts the BoC’s ability to acquire T-bills without causing distortions in bill rates. As a result, the BoC tends to increase lending through overnight or term repo operations when settlement balances decrease and repo rates rise. The BoC does not currently operate daily overnight repo operations but instead steps in when CORRA is uncomfortably above their policy target (typically target rate +5bp). Receiver General Auctions: shift liquidity Although not a facility directly controlled by the BoC, the Bank acts as fiscal agent for the GoC by managing excess cash in the Receiver General (RG) account. This is accomplished through daily RG auctions, which differ from other BoC lending operations. Specifically, RG auctions do not expand the size of the BoC’s balance sheet; instead, they shift liquidity with the BoC’s balance sheet liabilities from the GoC’s deposits into settlement balances. records.text: Global Strategy15 June 2026 ab 14 'Supportive': Rising volatilities from low levels should support option-like strategies There is a natural and well-studied connection between trend-following and long- volatility strategies. Both are characterized by a positive convexity and positive skewness, which make them strong candidates for tail hedging. Jean-Philippe Bouchaud & co have shown mathematically in their paper Tail protection for long investors: trend convexity at work that trend following strategies have exactly the same exposure to the long-term variance (large moves unfolding over several weeks/months) as a portfolio of naked strangles. This relationship is particularly relevant today, as cross-asset volatility and index correlations remain subdued despite heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Any normalization higher in volatility would likely benefit option-like strategies. Figure 27: Index correlations are currently at extreme levels, with scope to rise over the next 12 months. Refer to important disclosures on page 17 to 18. 12983773 Japan Viewpoint BoJ watching 101: Economics and Rates Primer BoJ mandate, 2% target, and institutional setting The BoJ’s monetary policy mandate is price stability. The Bank of Japan Act sets no numerical inflation target; the current 2% target was adopted by the Policy Board in January 2013, alongside a Joint Statement with the government. The institutional setting is also important: the BoJ decides policy independently, but the Act calls for close coordination with the government so that monetary policy and the basic stance of the government’s economic policy remain mutually compatible. How the BoJ sets policy in practice Policy is decided by majority vote at Monetary Policy Meetings of the nine-member Policy Board. In practice, the BoJ does not run a mechanical reaction function or set rates against a single estimate of neutral. Instead, it asks whether underlying inflation is becoming anchored around 2% in a sustainable and stable manner. GDP growth (quarterly at annualised rates) has averaged 1.4% since Q4 2019, outpacing the Eurozone and France (each 1.2%) and above all Germany (0.2%). Only Spain has registered stronger growth, on average (2.3%). This is despite both Italy and Spain registering the sharpest decline in GDP in the Eurozone during the Covid crisis in H1 2020. The performance this decade contrasts sharply with the prior two decades, when Italy was the growth laggard among the large Eurozone countries, with average growth of 0.4% and 0.2%, respectively. As a result of this transaction, and combined with the benefits of the tender offer on the short end of the curve, CARLB bonds 33s and 35s have tightened by c.10bp since then and now trade inside high-BBB peers and closer to low-A issuers (Figure 20). This is overdone, in our view, especially as Carlsberg has just regained financial leeway within a Baa1 rating, while the effective deleveraging from cash flow generation is still to come. CARLB 33s and 35s now trade just on top of HEIANA curve, which is better rated (BBB+ Pos/A3); CARLB 33s trade in line with CCEP 33s - which was upgraded to A3 by Moody's earlier this year - and in line with CARLB 3.25% 2032 for a one year longer maturity and a higher cash price. Therefore, at current spread levels, we would prefer Heineken and CCEP to CARLB and recommend taking profit and selling CARLB 4.25% 2033 (at 103.5, z+69) in particular. Furthermore, we would also prefer the new CARLB 4.875% NC34 hybrid bond issued in May, which offers a c.110bp pick up vs CARLB 33s and a YTC of 4.8%, while staying IG-rated, hence our trade idea to switch out of CARLB 4.25% 2033 into CARLB 4.875% NC34-Perp. We see this instrument as a better way to take a position on the brewer ahead of the summer season and FIFA World Cup than senior bonds. 17 June 2026 16 Barclays | European IG Best Ideas

While we expect the MPC to leave its options open for July, given conflict uncertainty, another hold seems most likely, in our view. Even with a hawkish shift in the vote split, we expect the overall rhetoric to allow the pricing for July to start to fade, too. One caveat here is that there could be more new information in next week’s data—with inflation due on 17 June and labour market data on 18 June—than in the MPC meeting itself. As it stands, we still find it more likely that the ECB, rather than the MPC, hike in July (see here for thoughts on the ECB), hence sticking to being received Jul26 MPC SONIA vs paid Jul26 ECB €STR (current 157.8bp, 13:30 BST 12Jun26) targeting 145bp. If there is a hike, the autumn seems more likely than July, as priced. A hike in July is now priced at 30% chance, but that is now lower than the 40% probability attached to September and November – Figure 16. We’d agree with the market sentiment that, should there be a hike, it is most likely around the autumn should higher oil prices prove persistent. records.text: eased six business days after each MPM, the Summary of Opinions (SoO) provides an early, anonymized read on Policy Board views. The SoO was introduced in 2016 under Governor Kuroda in response to market concerns about the long lag to the MPM minutes. Each Policy Board member and government attendee summarizes the views they expressed at the meeting in no more than 300 Japanese characters. The Governor, as chair, then edits the submissions by topic. Individual views are presented separately, without attribution. The document is organized into three sections: (i) economic and financial developments, (ii) monetary policy, and (iii) government views. The character limit forces participants to prioritize what they consider most important. The key is to read the balance of emphasis across sections and the extent to which particular points appear to be shared across the Board. A greater weight on prices or monetary policy can show where the Board’s attention is focused, but it does not by itself signal a policy change at the next meeting. References to monetary policy also tend to increase in meetings where policy is changed, but that mainly reflects the nature of the discussion at those meetings and has limited predictive value for future decisions.

records.text: ge is to stabilize underlying inflation around 2%. Policy is therefore based on a comprehensive assessment of prices, wages, activity, and financial conditions, rather than an explicit reaction-function rule. No mechanical policy rules Monetary policy rules have been discussed in Policy Board deliberations before, with the Taylor rule debate during Ueda’s first stint as a Board member in the late 1990s to early 2000s a notable example. But no specific monetary policy rule has ever been adopted as an operating guide. The closest the Bank has come to a rule-based commitment was Kuroda’s September 2016 inflation-overshooting commitment under QQE with Yield Curve Control. This functioned as a duration commitment to maintain accommodation until inflation exceeded 2%, rather than a reaction function for policy settings. The natural rate of interest (R*) serves as a rough reference rather than a hard anchor. As of 3Q 2025, the six-model range for R* compiled by the Monetary Affairs Department was around -0.9% to +0.5%. In addition to the wide dispersion across models, these estimates are subject to large ex-post revisions and likely downward bias in Japan, given the long period at the effective lower bound. Recent Bank communication does not treat R* as a mechanical guide to the policy rate. Where rates settle depends on a broader assessment of financial conditions, the output gap, and progress on inflation anchoring.

Prima facie, this may seem paradoxical; after all, gold is supposed to rally in times of acute geopolitical upheaval due to its safe-haven properties. In what follows, we show that the recent sell-off is a by-product of the interplay between gold’s various underlying drivers and crowded positioning. That said, we also argue that US inflation – gold’s dominant influence over the medium to long term – points to a rebound ahead, once geopolitics stabilise. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 15 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Will the BoJ be hawkish enough? The BoJ should tighten this week. But if they still sound dovish relative to its peers, markets may challenge whether FX and monetary policy are as consistent as they can be. The latest bout of JPY weakness began nine months ago, driven by the view that the new government would resist tighter monetary policy, favouring expansionary fiscal policy and easier monetary settings. This week that narrative almost flips. In recent months the MoF has sanctioned intervention to lean against JPY weakness; the question now is whether the BoJ will be hawkish enough to support that stance. Japan’s macro-outlook, unlike elsewhere, is largely unchanged. Controlled fuel prices have left current inflation and forecasts little changed (Figure 1), while recent economic data has generally surprised on the upside. That leaves the BoJ with the same challenge it faced at the start of the year: how quickly to move rates back to neutral. Unlike most major central banks, the BoJ still has rates below its own estimates of neutral (Figure 2). Only the SNB has similarly accommodative policy, and it is battling an overvalued, not undervalued, currency. This relative stability in Japan’s outlook has, oddly, become a challenge. records.text: Equity Derivatives Strategy: Gold down from h(e)aven Anshul Gupta Barclays, UK | Stefano Pascale BCI, US A crowded upside chase gives way to a technical reset... Gold's recent pull-back marks a clear reset after an extended, technically stretched rally from earlier this year, which had increasingly attracted "bubble" narratives, with many of the classic hallmarks, such as a pronounced spot-up/vol-up dynamic (Figure 15), deeply inverted call skews, and crowded positioning, all indicative of an aggressive upside chase. ...with options and positioning dynamics normalising meaningfully. The backdrop has since shifted meaningfully, with option pricing, sentiment, and positioning normalising from early- year extremes. Implied volatility has normalised from peak levels, albeit remaining elevated. More importantly, the skew dynamics have reversed sharply, with call skew no longer inverted and, in fact, call options now screening as carrying the least premium relative to ATM in a decade (Figure 17). At the same time, put skew has steepened, signalling a pivot towards increased hedging demand (Figure 18). Similarly, on the retail demand side, precious metals saw the steepest 2-week outflows in 1Q26 (Figure 19). The timing of these flows suggests sentiment had already rolled over well before the recent move higher in global yields, underscoring the importance of speculative appetite beyond the standard macro drivers of real rates and the USD in shaping gold’s performance. All Deputy Governors are full members of the Council and share responsibility for monetary policy decisions. External Deputy Governors were introduced in 2023 to bring outside perspectives to monetary policy and financial stability discussions. The MPRC, which includes these members along with advisors and senior staff, supports the process by reviewing analysis and offering recommendations. Input is based on both internal assessments and external sources of information. The decision-making framework is organized into four main stages: 1. Presentation of staff projections and economic briefing: Around three weeks before the decision, staff present forecasts for the Canadian and global economies, as well as inflation and commodity trends, including associated risks and alternative scenarios; economic departments provide updates on domestic and international developments, financial stability, credit conditions, and market activity, while surveys and regional data add further context. 2. records.text: Canada Viewpoint | 15 June 2026 3 The BoC also estimates the neutral rate and the potential output to further guide its decisions. The neutral rate and the potential output are updated yearly in April’s MPR (Monetary Policy Report). The current nominal neutral rate is estimated at 2.25%–3.25%, unchanged from the 2025 evaluation, as offsetting forces—higher productivity growth and lower population growth—balance out. Given Canada’s status as a small open economy, global conditions are critical and the US neutral rate is used as a proxy of the neutral global rate. The most recent estimation for the US range was revised upward to 2.50%–3.50%, reflecting stronger expected productivity linked to AI, but partly offset by weaker population growth. Potential output is projected to grow by 1.2% in 2026, rising to 1.5% by 2028. This gradual increase reflects stable labor input amid aging and subdued population growth, alongside productivity gains averaging 1.4%, supported in part by AI adoption. Decision-making framework The BoC sets its policy interest rate on eight scheduled dates each year, typically spaced six to seven weeks apart. In unusual situations, it may adjust the rate outside this timetable, as was the case in March 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. The process involves the Governing Council, the Monetary Policy Review Committee (MPRC), and four economics departments. Action calculation: FOMC OIS makes it very straightforward to compute implied odds of a Fed action. For example, to compute the probability of Fed action at the July meeting simply take the difference between July & June FOMC OIS & divide by 25bps. Fed funds futures: monthly contracts Fed funds (FF) futures contracts are another tool to access market pricing for Fed path. FF futures are CME listed contracts that reflect the average FF reported by the FRBNY rate over a calendar month. The contract is settled against the average FF effective rate for each date in the delivery month. Fed funds futures are typically liquid out to 6M; thereafter there is a substantial decline in open interest out to 1Y. Open interest is typically very limited beyond 1Y forward tenors. Like FOMC OIS, these contracts reflect FF moves within the target range and use the last day for which a rate was published to account for weekends and holidays. records.text: June FOMC Recap: Hikes Look More Likely but Are Still Not Our Base Case As widely expected, the FOMC left the funds rate unchanged at 3.5-3.75% today and removed the previous forward guidance suggesting cuts from its statement at the June FOMC meeting today. The FOMC also substantially shortened and simplified its post-meeting statement. But the meeting also delivered a significant hawkish surprise, with nine participants projecting a rate hike in 2026, against our expectation that just three would. Because the new Chairman Kevin Warsh chose not to submit projections, this resulted in a nine to nine tie in the dot plot between those projecting at least one hike and those projecting an unchanged policy rate or, in one case, a rate cut. Consistent with the hawkish message from the dots, the key surprise in the economic projections was that the median forecast for 2027 Q4/Q4 core PCE inflation rose 0.3pp to 2.5%, above our expectation that it would rise more modestly to 2.3%. This suggests that participants were more concerned that the recent firmer inflation news, caused in part by the energy cost shock from the war with Iran, has implications for inflation further down the road. It was not clear where Warsh stood on the likelihood of a hike being appropriate from the press conference. records.text: 2 US Viewpoint | 14 June 2026 The Fed’s dual mandate In 1977, Congress passed the Federal Reserve Reform Act following a period of elevated inflation and high unemployment. The act officially established what we know today as the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices. Congress also included a third goal of moderate long-term interest rates, but this is often seen as a byproduct of the first two goals and a stable macroeconomic environment. Federal Reserve Act: Monetary policy objectives The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Federal Open Market Committee shall maintain long run growth of the monetary and credit aggregates commensurate with the economy’s long run potential to increase production, so as to promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates. The dual mandate can lead to trade-offs The Fed’s dual mandate is unusual: most other central banks only target inflation. The dual mandate can lead to trade-offs in the short run. Rate hikes tend to lower inflation and raise unemployment, while cuts do the opposite. This inverse relationship is captured by the Phillips curve (Exhibit 1). The trade-off gets particularly challenging when the economy is hit by supply shocks. records.text: 16, 2026. • Frequency of use: The Securities Lending Facility was utilized 501 times in FY2023 and 488 times in both FY2024 and FY2025, and continues to be used. The SLF is conducted whenever one or more counterparties submit a request. • Auction method: A multiple-price competitive auction is conducted for each sale. In these auctions, domestic financial institutions bid “selling yields” (yields for the period during which securities are held by counterparties). Bids with lower selling yields are accepted first. • Upper limit on selling yields: The yield will be capped at the previous trading day’s Tokyo repo rate minus the minimum fee rate of 0.5%, effective July 16, 2026. The facility functions as a repo transaction between the BoJ and domestic banks— effectively, from the perspective of private institutions, borrowing JGBs from the BoJ while lending funds. Within this framework, the selling yield will be set 50bp below the GC repo rate. As a result, the return from using the facility is lower than that from investing funds in the GC repo market. The BoJ states that this design— specifically the minimum fee—aims to discourage excessive reliance on the facility by market participants. • Option to reduce repurchases (Gengaku Sochi): Financial institutions that purchase JGBs from the BoJ can pay a fee to request a reduction in the repurchase amount (by up to 100%) if they do not have the JGBs to deliver. By aggregating money-market funds and demand deposits relative to US equity market capitalisation, the figures provide a useful proxy for how much deployable liquidity exists versus the size of the asset base it can influence. At present, this ratio remains elevated, suggesting that cash buffers are still substantial and retain the capacity to support risk assets. Historically, this measure has been closely linked to forward return distributions: when cash balances are high relative to market cap, the marginal impact of reallocations into equities tends to be more powerful, supporting both returns and resilience to shocks. The current backdrop therefore points to a liquidity environment that remains broadly supportive, even if more vulnerable to short-term dislocations. One caveat is that not all cash is equal - some portion may be implicitly tied to leveraged positioning (via options, ETFs or margin), where drawdowns can quickly erode balance sheet capacity. This creates the potential for episodic fragility even within an otherwise liquid system. From a broader perspective, this still-robust liquidity backdrop is important not just for US markets, but globally. Strong US liquidity supports US demand, financial conditions, and ultimately global growth – all of which feed directly into European earnings. As Figure 3 shows, earlier bouts of intervention to support the JPY were usually followed by less dovish rhetoric from the central bank, keeping monetary and FX policy aligned. The problem is that most other central banks, especially the Fed, have turned notably more hawkish in response to the war- driven inflation shock (Figure 4). Historically, when the Fed is more hawkish than the BoJ, as it is today, the JPY weakens against the USD 67% of the time. When the BoJ sounds more hawkish, the JPY weakens only 29% of the time. The implication is straightforward: the BoJ will tighten this week, but if it still sounds dovish relative to the Fed later in the week, especially if it does not encourage markets to price further hikes this year, the balance of risks will favour a weaker JPY and test the authorities’ resolve to lean against it. Policy stasis : While we may start to get a sense of how Warsh intends to put his stamp on the Fed, we do not expect any of that aspiration to make their way into this week’s policy decisions. In many ways, the new Chair will try to establish his legacy with a clean slate by maintaining the current hold that has been in place since the start of the year. As discussed below, uncertain price transmission dynamics will continue to justify the upward policy bias adopted by investors. Additionally, the relative s trength in the economy has kept growth headwinds at bay for the time being, as reflected by both market and media measures of policy direction. As shown in Figure 1, media readings for the Fed had shifted hawkishly well before the start of the war, preceding overall policy pricing, which did not pivot until after the war started. In addition, options pricing still favours an even more hawkish 2+ hikes outcome this year relative to any dovish outcome of no changes or cuts. We would also note that media readi ngs on Warsh are generally hawkish relative to Powell, pushing back on the view that the Chair will be automatically dovish because of political bias. Overall, this will keep policy balanced at this meeting, with no change in rate or balance sheet policy. There are two broad narratives at play. The first is the ability of fiscal interventions to mechanically alter the path of CPI – a tool that is increasingly being used by the Treasury. However, we think there is minimal policy spillover for Bank of England given their preference to look through short-term effects (such as altering the energy price cap in the Autumn Budget). More concerning, in our view, would be the indirect effects of such policy interventions should they spill into the real economy. The most obvious space where this is relevant is in energy policy and on household energy bills. We have written in more detail about this (see: UK Economics - The fiscal implications of energy prices). While the numbers in that note are dated, the logic of the argument holds. The immediate consequence of such a policy would be to effectively cap energy bills and thus lower headline CPI over the short term. This mechanical change, for the MPC, would be less relevant than the knock-on effect implicit within it. As a result, investors increasingly emphasized the importance of isolating pure momentum effects after controlling for sector and factor exposures. Without decomposing performance drivers, it becomes difficult to determine whether returns are being driven by momentum itself, AI exposure, or simply higher beta. Another important distinction is between price momentum and earnings momentum. Several investors argued that given the possibility that the current AI rally could reverse in the future, greater emphasis should be placed on stocks supported by underlying fundamentals. We agree with this view. One candidate is earnings momentum, or the revision factor. During the dot-com bubble, the 12-month price momentum factor experienced a significant correction after the market peak, whereas revision factors remained relatively resilient. We highlighted this point in our May 14 report, Are We Going Back to 1999? Unlike pure price momentum, revision factors have demonstrated persistent effectiveness in the Japanese equity market over the medium to long term. records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY Un autre mois s’est écoulé alors que le conflit au Moyen-Orient – qui a désormais dépassé la barre des 100 jours – reste non résolu, le détroit d’Ormuz étant effectivement fermé. Pourtant, la perspective persistante d’un accord de paix éventuel et l’optimisme autour des gains liés à l’adoption de l’IA ont soutenu l’économie mondiale et les marchés. Nos prévisions économiques ont été élaborées en partant du principe que les cours du pétrole moyen seraient d’environ 110 USD / baril au cours du deuxième trimestre, puis chuteraient à environ 85 USD / baril au quatrième trimestre. Selon ces hypothèses, la croissance du PIB mondial ralentirait d’environ 0,5 point de pourcentage cette année, mais nous considérerions toujours le contexte de croissance global comme résilient. Jusqu’à présent au deuxième trimestre, les prix du pétrole ont évolué en moyenne à 102 USD / baril – un peu en dessous de notre hypothèse, mais conforme au récit de résilience. La suite dépendra en définitive de l’évolution du conflit – une résolution immédiate, un allongement du statu-quo fragile ou une escalade qui risquerait d’endommager davantage les infrastructures énergétiques clés. Une résolution immédiate pourrait faire chuter rapidement les prix du pétrole à 70 USD / baril, les primes de risque étant réduites et les cargaisons bloquées libérées, tandis qu’une escalade pourrait pousser les prix à 200 USD / baril. The JPY looks most vulnerable, and we raise our already above-consensus USDJPY forecast to 165 by year-end (previously 160). For EURUSD, we turn from bullish to neutral. We now see the pair trading at 1.16 by year end (previously 1.21). Cyclical factors apply downward pressure, but that should be offset by structural shifts among European investors. We see EURUSD trending higher in 2027. High-yielding EM FX can continue to trade well in this environment, in our view, especially with fundamentals remaining strong (see Macro: EM–DM divide is fading, dated 23 February). Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: We expect the Fed’s next policy move to be a rate hike, aimed at withdrawing the monetary stimulus provided by last year’s three ‘insurance’ cuts. This year’s strong growth, gradually tightening labor market and persistently high inflation strike us as markedly different conditions to those anticipated by officials at the time of last fall’s cuts, and we expect policy to adjust accordingly. We therefore expect that the main rationale for hikes will be to make good on a miscalibration.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 The amount of equity repo outstanding is a helpful proxy of how much leverage is being intermediated through dealer balance sheets into the broader equity market. • As shown in Exhibit 5 , total outstanding US primary dealer equity financing in repo hit a record high of $223bn in the week ended June 3. A natural question investors may ask is: is this simply a function of higher equity prices? In Exhibit 6 , we show the S&P 500 alongside the total amount of outstanding US primary dealer equity financing in repo since June 2022. • Indeed, increases in risky asset prices have necessitated additional capital dedicated to prime brokerage business responsible for meeting investors' equity financing needs. Hence, the continued growth in dealer equity repo exposure. In a backdrop where prime brokerage balance sheet capacity is just meeting the demand for levered long equity financing then it would not be an indication of market fragility. • But when US primary dealer equity financing repo exposure pushes to a record high, alongside squeezes higher in equity financing costs, it implies risk markets are becoming increasingly reliant on a scarce, finite resource. We address the question of whether record dealer equity repo financing exposure is driven by investor capital growth or increased leverage utilization per dollar of capital. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 3 Coordination with the government and accountability The 1997 Act preserved structured coordination between the BoJ and the government, reflecting the principle that monetary and fiscal policy should be broadly aligned. MoF and Cabinet Office representatives may attend Monetary Policy Meetings, express views, and submit proposals, but do not have voting rights. The government may request that the Policy Board postpone a decision, but the Board determines by majority vote whether to grant such requests. The January 2013 Joint Statement is the most visible expression of this framework, setting out shared objectives across the BoJ, MoF, and Cabinet Office. The BoJ also submits a “Semiannual Report on Currency and Monetary Control” covering its policy decisions and operations. BoJ officials appear before the Diet’s financial committees when requested to explain policy and respond to questions. Based on historical statistical relationships, we estimate that each 1% pullback in n real cash flow from an energy shock results in a 0.6% decline in consumer spending after two quarters. Our model is able to explain the limited consumption impact of higher energy prices so far but projects more meaningful weakness in H2, even with our new energy price forecasts. These predictions align with consumer surveys that show DM consumers anticipate making fewer large purchases over the next 6-12 months. Spending Headwinds Still to Come on Both Sides of the Pond The interim US-Iran peace deal has diminished upside tail risks to energy prices: our oil strategists now see Brent declining to $80 per barrel in 2026Q4 (vs. $90 previously) and our gas strategists also forecast slightly lower near-term prices (although they leave their year-end forecasts unchanged due to inventory rebuilding). Moreover, consumer spending has so far held up reasonably well on both sides of the Atlantic since the start of the conflict (Exhibit 1). While these are both welcome developments for the growth outlook, we see three reasons why it is too early for complacency on real income and consumer spending. BoJ and FX interventions Context In Japan, foreign exchange (FX) policy is set by the Ministry of Finance (MoF), not the Bank of Japan. The authority to conduct FX intervention rests with the Minister of Finance, and exchange rate policy is treated as a government decision rather than a monetary policy tool. The BoJ’s role is operational: it acts as the government’s agent, executing interventions at the instruction of the MoF. The Bank provides market intelligence and settlement functions but has no independent authority to intervene. Mechanism Against this backdrop, interventions are conducted through the government’s Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account (FEFSA). Specifically, in the case of yen-selling/US$-purchasing interventions, dollars are bought using yen funds raised through the issuance of Financing Bills (FBs). Meanwhile, US$-selling/yen-buying operations are conducted by selling the US dollars held in the FEFSA in exchange for yen.

records.text: 8 Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 How to read media reports Pre-MPM press reports flagging likely policy moves and forecast changes are a regular feature of the BoJ cycle, and some market participants describe them as “leaks” from the Bank. In practice, they should usually be read less as direct leaks than as reporting built from multiple inputs. BoJ beat reporters at Nikkei, Jiji, Kyodo, Reuters, Bloomberg, and the major Japanese dailies receive regular background briefings, known in Japanese as reku (レク), on the policy framework and context. They cross-check those briefings against their own source networks at the BoJ, MoF, the Prime Minister’s Office, and political circles, as well as signals from BoJ communications. Most “BoJ sources say” reporting is therefore best understood as a synthesis of background briefings, the reporter’s own sourcing, and their reading of BoJ communications, rather than a leak in the strict sense. Frameworks to assess policy setting The BoJ’s monetary policy objective is the sustainable and stable achievement of its 2% price stability target. Like other central banks, it eases when inflation is below target and activity is weak, and tightens when the opposite holds. What makes Japan different is that, after a long period of undershooting, the challenge is to stabilize underlying inflation around 2%. records.text: For the first time in many decades, the demand for capital is rising. The private sector is ramping up capex and infrastructure spending in order to support and power the AI revolution, and to build more reliable and robust supply chains. Concurrently, governments are spending more to strengthen capacity in defence and critical infrastructure. A higher cost of capital caps equity valuations, making fundamental earnings growth more important; it should also increase the differentiation of returns across companies, making alpha increasingly important relative to beta. Equity market implications of the ‘Post Modern’ cycle For most of the period that followed the financial crisis, the combination of growth scarcity and ultra low discount rates widened the valuation and performance spread between growth companies and those in more mature industries. Cheap cost of capital meant investors were willing to fund companies with strong growth prospects, particularly in the tech sector, where costs were low. It was a period in which the benefits of the Internet revolution were beginning to bear fruit. Leading companies in software and cloud computing began to grow and scale as the digital revolution deepened. These companies were able to generate particularly high returns on investment and benefited from the capex that emerged during the dotcom bubble a decade earlier. records.text: Middle East conflict boosts Panama Canal traffic: The Panama Canal is a critical chokepoint for global trade, handling around 5% of global maritime commerce. It is especially important for the US: about 70% of vessels transiting the canal either depart from or head to US ports, while more than 40% of annual US container traffic transits this waterway. The blockade around the Strait of Hormuz has driven a surge in US energy exports to Asia, leading to increased demand for transit slots in the Panama Canal. Baltic and International Maritime Council analysis showed that canal traffic had risen by 8% y/y as at 21 May, reaching an average of 38 daily transits. Auction prices had also increased sharply, while average waiting times had risen by 50% y/y to 47 hours. Water crunch from El Niño: The Panama Canal is uniquely exposed to climatic conditions, as its operations depend entirely on freshwater from Gatun Lake. Ships pass through a series of locks that use lake water to raise vessels above sea level before lowering them again on the other side. During El Niño events, lower rainfall can reduce Gatun Lake water levels, limiting the number of vessels that can pass through the canal. El Niño-related droughts in 1997–98, 2015–16 and 2023–24 had disrupted canal traffic, leading to transit restrictions, vessel delays and higher transportation costs. We subsequently push our expected cuts back, with the first landing in late Q2 2027 and then in Q3, with an unchanged terminal rate of 3.25%. We give a detailed exposition on why by shedding light on the MPC’s reaction function drawing from what they said in the April MPR and public remarks. However, we think the June policy statement will continue to read as hawkish and, indeed, we explain why we believe Megan Greene will join Huw Pill to also vote for a hike this time. A renewed challenge for the MPC — Yet another stagflationary environment seems to be emerging in the UK economy. On the one hand, the underlying variables are weakening. On the other hand, the threat of higher energy prices leaking into CPI components and nominal wages is making them wary of repeating the same policy error of 2022/23. While we think a hold is likely, the risks still point up — Our base case has the BoE on hold for the rest of the year, with the next move likely a cut. records.text: e: UBS, Machine Learning model At the aggregate level, consensus expectations have become increasingly optimistic, with European EPS growth now forecast at c.15-16% for 2026 after several years of near-zero growth. However, this recovery is highly concentrated: Financials remain the dominant contributor to earnings growth, with energy providing a growing incremental boost more recently. Importantly, for the first time since 2021, there are no sectors acting as a drag on aggregate earnings growth, a notable shift from prior periods when energy and consumer discretionary weighed meaningfully. That said, this breadth likely overstates the true strength of the earnings cycle. Upgrades to growth estimates have been concentrated in a small subset of sectors, while most others are already experiencing steady downgrades, with cost pressures and weak demand beginning to compress margins.

It is an early adopter, having introduced the framework in 1991; since then, inflation has averaged 2.1%. Policy is forward‑looking, with decisions guided by projected inflation over a six‑ to eight‑quarter horizon and a broad assessment of economic conditions. Core measures (CPI‑trim and CPI‑median) are key inputs, and policy is designed to look through transitory shocks within a flexible FX regime. The BoC also considers its estimates of the neutral rate and potential output. Economics: Consensus-based policymaking Policy decisions are the responsibility of the Governing Council, while the Board of Directors oversees governance and operations. records.text: a market perspective, momentum performs best in an environment of low but gradually rising volatility and stock correlations, elevated real rates, and central bank pricing beginning to turn more dovish from tight levels. Most of these conditions are present today, with one notable exception: the Fed is currently being priced more hawkishly. Should the Fed signal the possibility of a full hiking cycle, momentum could face a short-term correction. Beyond this risk, however, the outlook for momentum strategies remains constructive. Watching earnings revisions in AI enablers is key over the medium term Momentum strategies tend to perform best when a small number of sectors lead the market during secular bull phases. Today, momentum has effectively become synonymous with the AI trade. Encouragingly, the current cycle is more driven by earnings growth than in previous episodes, which increases the likelihood of its durability. At the same time, the key risk is clear: any deterioration in earnings revisions for AI enablers would challenge both momentum and the broader market. This report has been prepared by UBS Europe SE. records.text: come shock. Fiscal and political outlook The upcoming by-election in Makerfield on 18 June is the next key event for UK’s political and fiscal outlook. There are many potential scenarios, but if Andy Burnham were to win, he would become eligible to stand in a Labour leadership contest. In such a leadership contest, a Survation poll suggests that Andy Burnham is viewed as favourite to win. Political uncertainty has increased near term policy uncertainty and somewhat tighter financial conditions, which could weigh on growth. Markets are likely to price in broad policy continuity if Starmer remains as PM or if Streeting is the next leader. Commitment to fiscal rules is likely in this scenario. Having said that, fiscal pressures are high even in this scenario on energy, public services (current plans imply real-terms cuts to unprotected day-to-day spending from 2028/29) and defence spending pressures. And in any case the fiscal space has reduced- we estimate that since March, the fiscal headroom has been reduced by close to £10bn from £23.6bn. A soft left leaning candidate could raise questions on whether fiscal rules are adhered to. So far commentary from soft left is that fiscal rules are likely to be met, which we would expect in the near term to avoid a negative market reaction. But it may get more complicated in the medium term. Some in the soft left have suggested tweaks in the fiscal framework, which can increase risks of a rise in borrowing. But a key reason consumption and investment has slowed is policy changes, especially the reduction in fiscal subsides, the imposition of auto purchase tax on EVs and the anti-involution campaign which discourages massive subsides for retail sales and new capex projects. To this extent, deteriorating structure is the cost that must be paid for better growth quality. The semi -annual Politburo Economic meeting is likely to be held in late July, at which economic works for H2 would be mapped out. We expect government bond issuance and corresponding fiscal spending, which have been slow in H1, to be stepped up in Q3, to counteract some of the downward pressure on growth. However, we think incremental fiscal and semi -fiscal measures, such as granting additional quota for special LGB issuance and/or the new policy-based financial instrument, are only likely to be considered in Q4 if economic downside risks continue to heighten at a time when most of the fiscal bullets budgeted for 2026 have been exhausted . As for monetary policy, given unabated pressure on bank net interest margins, and a shift from deflation to mild reflation, we think the People’s Bank of China will not cut its policy rate or the RRR over the course of 2026. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 7 The better use of the SoO is to check whether points emphasized in the Governor’s post-MPM press conference were broadly reflected in Board discussion and to track how the policy debate is shifting over time. It should not be read as a document designed to signal the next policy move directly. Minutes (議事要旨) The MPM minutes are released after approval at the subsequent MPM. The timing depends on the interval between meetings, but is typically around seven to eight weeks after the original meeting. They provide a more comprehensive account of the discussion than the Summary of Opinions, while still keeping speakers anonymous. The minutes use qualifiers such as “many members,” “several members,” and “one member,” giving some indication of how widely particular views were shared across the Policy Board. Compared with the Summary of Opinions, the MPM minutes have more of the character of an official record of the meeting. They are more comprehensive, but the longer publication lag limits their usefulness for near-term policy read-through. Full transcripts (議事録), including speaker names and remarks, are released with a ten- year lag. Non‑MPM communication Speeches and regional addresses (金融経済懇談会) The main channel for inter‑meeting signaling and the most frequent communication output of the Bank.
