records.text: The most important change in the economic data since the last FOMC meeting is n the impressive pick-up in job growth that has put the labor market on a sturdier trajectory. This has left the focus on whether the inflation situation is becoming concerning enough to warrant a rate hike. The war and the increase in oil prices will likely drive headline PCE inflation above 4% and leave core PCE inflation above 3% all year. But so far the impact on inflation looks more like the usual passthrough from large oil shocks than the pandemic’s wide-ranging shortages and price spikes. We continue to see rate hikes as unlikely, both because the Fed has usually not n hiked in response to oil price shocks in the past, and because conditions today, especially the more balanced state of the labor market, make it less likely that the oil shock will spark self-sustaining high inflation. That said, there have been some concerning signs already, and meaningful increases in inflation expectations or the breadth of high inflation across categories would make a hike more likely. At its June meeting, the first under new Chairman Kevin Warsh, the FOMC is likely n to keep the funds rate unchanged and drop the previous forward guidance suggesting cuts. A number of major central banks meet this week, needing to assess the latest developments around the US-Iran 60-day Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz - and the resulting impact on energy prices - will be central to that assessment. Current expectations are that the strait will fully reopen within 30 days of the agreement being signed. A meaningful and sustained decline in energy prices would give policymakers greater confidence that inflation expectations will remain anchored. The key question is whether the damage has already been done for some economies, or whether central banks can credibly frame the shock as transitory. In our view, it is too early for central banks to alter this week’s policy plans; they are more likely to signal a wait-and-see approach. The main event will be the Federal Reserve meeting, where new Chair Kevin Warsh makes his debut. The policy statement, SEP, and dot plot are likely to lean moderately hawkish, although the press conference leaves room for surprises. Warsh could use it to lay the groundwork for changes to Fed communications, highlight his preferred inflation measure and outline his views on the balance sheet. records.text: June FOMC Preview: Leadership Transition The most important change in the economic data since the last FOMC meeting is the impressive pick-up in job growth that has put the labor market on a much sturdier trajectory. While we still expect somewhat below-potential GDP growth in the second half of this year as high oil prices weigh on spending, we expect the unemployment rate to rise only a touch further to 4.4% (Exhibit 1). The better labor market data allow the FOMC to focus on whether the inflation situation is becoming concerning enough to warrant a rate hike. The war and the increase in oil prices will likely drive headline PCE inflation above 4% and leave core PCE inflation above 3% all year, even as the effects of last year’s tariff increases gradually drop out of the year-over-year calculation (Exhibit 2). But so far the impact on inflation looks more like the usual passthrough from large oil shocks than the pandemic’s wide-ranging shortages and price spikes. We think that we have likely now moved through the most extreme effects of the increase in oil prices and in computer memory prices sparked by AI demand on the monthly pace of inflation, which we expect to decline in the remainder of the year. records.text: 4 Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 Policy Board composition The Board is led by Governor Kazuo Ueda, who took office in April 2023 as the first academic to hold the post in the postwar era. He holds a PhD in economics from MIT, taught at the University of Tokyo, and previously served on the Policy Board from 1998 to 2005. His appointment broke with the longstanding unwritten convention that the governorship alternates between former MoF officials and career BoJ officials. His two Deputy Governors are Shinichi Uchida, a career BoJ official, and Ryozo Himino, a former Commissioner of the Financial Services Agency. The other six Policy Board seats have traditionally reflected a balance of backgrounds. Typically, this has meant at least one member from the major banks, one from securities, and one from industry, with the remaining seats filled more flexibly. This reflects an unwritten convention that the Board should represent constituencies affected by monetary policy. Since the early 2020s, there has been a clear shift toward more academic members. Ueda, Koeda, Asada, and Sato are all drawn from academia rather than the financial industry; Sato joins the Policy Board on 30 June 2026, replacing Nakagawa, whose term ends at that time. The next few years are consequential for the Board’s composition. Two further vacancies are expected in 2027, and the terms of Ueda, Uchida, and Himino all expire in March-April 2028. Recent central bank communication is now consis- tent with a period of cash rate stability and we think rate cuts are likely from mid-2027. The Fed holds eight scheduled meetings per year; it can also hold unscheduled meetings when needed. At each meeting, committee members vote on the policy action, including changes to the official statement that follows the meeting. Members can dissent against the action or the wording of the statement (Exhibit 3). The Chair’s vote does not carry any more weight than other votes. Governors: nominated by President, confirmed by Senate The selection of Governors is up to the US President. Each Governor is nominated by the President and then must be approved by the Senate (first by the Senate Banking Committee). Governor terms last for 14 years and the terms are staggered, with one ending on Jan 31 of every other year (the even-numbered years, e.g. Powell’s term as a Governor ends in 2028, see Exhibit 4). Governors can fill unexpired terms and then be nominated to fill a new 14-year term. The President also nominates and the Senate confirms the Chair and Vice Chair of the Federal Reserve, and the Vice Chair for Supervision. These positions are four-year terms, and the officials have the prerogative to remain on the Board as Governors thereafter, until their terms as Governors expire. 0% 1% 2% 3% 4% 5% 6% -5 0 5 10 Core PCE (% yoy) Unemployment rate gap (U-rate - NAIRU) 0 1 2 3 Nov- 2007 Nov- 2010 Sep- 2013 Sep- 2016 Sep- 2019 FOM- 2022 Dec- 2025 2

records.text: ab 15 June 2026 Global Research Global Strategy Stretched, But Not Yet Breaking: The Case for Staying with Momentum What the Momentum strategy is about Momentum strategies aim to capture the persistence, or inertia, in price trends, which typically reflects an extended profit cycle. Avoiding sharp turning points in the economic cycle and shifts in market leadership is therefore critical. Longer, uninterrupted cycles can be driven by structural forces, such as rising productivity expectations (e.g. globalisation in the 1990s), or supported by policy (loose monetary policy in the 2010s, fiscal expansion in the 2020s). Today, both fiscal support and optimism around AI-driven productivity are helping sustain the global cycle. While it remains early, if the risk of an oil-driven global recession has indeed been averted, momentum strategies appear to have already passed an important test. What kind of backdrop does Momentum work in? One broadly similar to today’s environment: we analyse seven episodes over the past three decades during which momentum significantly outperformed the market. The macro backdrop in which momentum tends to thrive is characterised by sustained economic expansion and above-average inflation, conditions more typical of the late cycle than the early cycle. This compression story is well flagged by the platforms; a significant competitive push could lead to a worse-than-expected outcome. Interest income treatment: In Sep-23, the FCA published its “Dear CEO” letter to investment platforms, in which it highlighted that interest income on customers’ cash balances should be carefully considered as part of fair value assessments. Global FX Strategy17 June 2026 ab 10 Global FX Strategy UBS Research AUD: Waiting game The technical backdrop for AUD has improved over recent months. Positioning has reset, carry-to-volatility metrics have strengthened, and RBA pricing is less demanding. In many respects, the conditions that led us to close our AUD long in March have reversed. However, at the same time, AUD currently has the highest sensitivity to US real rates in the G10; therefore, ahead of a highly uncertain FOMC meeting, we are holding off on adding AUD risk. In addition, a weaker housing outlook bears monitoring and may weaken the longer-term AUD outlook. We believe the risk-reward on AUD longs has improved, but we would prefer either better entry levels or greater clarity on the external outlook before re-engaging. Our preferred expression of AUD longs would be against low yielders, such as CHF. However, we do not like adding US rate beta ahead of a Fed meeting that has potentially wide- ranging implications. In this note we outline why the risk-reward has improved, and what is still holding us back. records.text: 10 Japan Viewpoint | 17 June 2026 On interest rates, it tracks the short-term policy rate, the JGB yield curve, and real interest rates across maturities to assess the interest-rate burden facing firms and households. In judging the effect on corporate financing, the BoJ has historically tended to focus on shorter tenors, particularly those of five years or less, which matter more directly for funding conditions. On the funding environment, the BoJ looks at funding costs (lending rates, CP and corporate bond issuance rates and spreads), availability of funds (Tankan diffusion indices for lending attitudes and firms’ financial positions), asset prices (equities, FX), and funding volumes (bank lending, CP, and corporate bonds outstanding). Taken together, these indicators show whether financial conditions remain accommodative or are tightening in response to policy changes. The real economy Slack is assessed primarily through the output gap, which summarizes excess or tight capacity in labor and capital. The BoJ also monitors labor-market indicators directly because stronger labor supply constraints have made labor-market balance more relevant for labor-intensive activity, wages, and prices. These indicators are used as complements to the output gap and include the Beveridge ratio, Tankan employment conditions DI, unemployment rate, employment rate gap, and job accession-separation gap. However, as seen in other themes such as EU defence, strong structural narratives can still underperform if earnings revisions stop surprising to the upside. The implication is that risks around AI capex are becoming more two-sided. If these emerging constraints limit how quickly spending can scale – or simply reduce the pace of further upgrades – the momentum underpinning the theme could fade. records.text: UK Economics and Rates 15 June 2026 Citi Research 10 The second and equally important thing to watch is the development of the political situation over summer. The Treasury is confronted with something of a fiscal ‘trilemma’ , where the competing pressures of higher spending, the fiscal rules, and a manifesto that inhibits capacity for large tax increases are forcing a trade-off in the political sphere between desirable and achievable policy. As the government faces the risk of a leadership challenge over the summer, this trade-off will increasingly become a battlefield as candidates lever fiscal as a political tool. It is unclear whether there is, absent any changes to the fiscal rules or further taxation, any capacity for a meaningful increase in expenditure. The autumn budget in 2025 attempted to deliver a convincing narrative of fiscal sustainability. As we noted at the time (see: UK Economics and Rates - 2025 Budget Preview: The Chancellor’s Gambit, and since: UK Economics and Rates - Spring Statement: Better, but riskier), the headroom against the primary fiscal rule was not enough to effectively insulate public finances from a large shock. This has driven fiscal policy towards something of an unvirtuous cycle, where a relative underperformance in UK debt compared with other European countries has eroded fiscal headroom and brought back the now-familiar discussion on how close the Chancellor is to breaching the rules.
